We hypothesize that (1) the brain optimizes cost functions, (2) the cost functions are diverse and differ across brain locations and over development, and (3) optimization operates within a pre-structured architecture matched to the computational problems posed by behavior. In support of these hypotheses, we argue that a range of implementations of credit assignment through multiple layers of neurons are compatible with our current knowledge of neural circuitry, and that the brain's specialized systems can be interpreted as enabling efficient optimization for specific problem classes. Such a heterogeneously optimized system, enabled by a series of interacting cost functions, serves to make learning data-efficient and precisely targeted to the needs of the organism. We suggest directions by which neuroscience could seek to refine and test these hypotheses.

papers.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
papers.research_question: What are the distinct training dynamics and phase transitions that occur at small versus large learning rates in deep networks, and how do they affect generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the catapult mechanism, a dynamical phase transition in training dynamics that allows deep networks to stably train at large learning rates, leading to flatter minima and improved generalization.
papers.conclusion: The catapult mechanism enables training at large learning rates by reducing curvature, leading to flatter minima and improved generalization, thereby bridging infinite-width theory and practical deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies three learning rate phases: lazy (η < 2/λ0), catapult (2/λ0 < η < η_max), and divergent (η > η_max), with distinct training dynamics.
In the catapult phase, the loss initially grows (catapult effect) while curvature rapidly decreases, after which training converges to a flat minimum.
The catapult phase often yields optimal generalization performance, and the maximum learning rate η_max is approximately 12/λ0 for ReLU networks.
Theoretical analysis shows that the catapult dynamics are non-perturbative and cannot be captured by linearized models or finite-width perturbative expansions.
Empirical validation across various architectures (fully-connected, convolutional, Wide ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) confirms the predicted phases and performance trends.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to MSE loss; extension to softmax classification is not explored.
Behavior for other optimizers such as SGD with momentum may differ and is not studied.
The simple model predicts maximum learning rate 4/λ0, but for ReLU networks it is higher (≈12/λ0), indicating possible separate mechanisms.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to softmax classification.
Study the effect of optimizers such as SGD with momentum.
Investigate the reason for the higher maximum learning rate in ReLU networks.
papers.abstract: The choice of initial learning rate can have a profound effect on the performance of deep networks. We present a class of neural networks with solvable training dynamics, and confirm their predictions empirically in practical deep learning settings. The networks exhibit sharply distinct behaviors at small and large learning rates. The two regimes are separated by a phase transition. In the small learning rate phase, training can be understood using the existing theory of infinitely wide neural networks. At large learning rates the model captures qualitatively distinct phenomena, including the convergence of gradient descent dynamics to flatter minima. One key prediction of our model is a narrow range of large, stable learning rates. We find good agreement between our model's predictions and training dynamics in realistic deep learning settings. Furthermore, we find that the optimal performance in such settings is often found in the large learning rate phase. We believe our results shed light on characteristics of models trained at different learning rates. In particular, they fill a gap between existing wide neural network theory, and the nonlinear, large learning rate, training dynamics relevant to practice.

papers.title: Advancing General Multimodal Capability of Vision-language Models with Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding
papers.research_question: How does visual position encoding affect the perception capabilities of Vision-language Models (VLMs), and can a novel encoding method mitigate limitations like long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern' to improve multi-granularity perception?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding (PyPE), a novel position assignment strategy for visual tokens in VLMs that assigns indexes from periphery to center and incrementally expands the central receptive field, mitigating long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern' to improve multi-granularity perception and reduce hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: PyPE effectively addresses limitations of conventional visual position encoding methods by mitigating long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern', leading to improved multi-granularity perception and overall performance of VLMs across diverse benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
PyPE consistently improves performance across various VQA and general multimodal benchmarks for VLMs of different sizes.
PyPE reduces object hallucinations and misunderstandings in generated descriptions compared to baseline position encoding methods.
The method alleviates the 'aggregation pattern' (over-reliance on anchor tokens) and enables more rational attention weight allocation.
PyPE demonstrates superior fine-grained perception while maintaining competitive coarse-grained perception capabilities.
A moderate descent interval (e.g., every 2 layers) generally provides the best balance of performance across tasks.
papers.limitation: PyPE is currently limited to single-frame images and has not yet been extended to video and other modalities.
future_direction: Effectively integrating the temporal dimension for unified position encoding in videos.
Extending PyPE to a broader range of VLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in advancing general artificial intelligence, yet the irrational encoding of visual positions persists in inhibiting the models' comprehensive perception performance across different levels of granularity. In this work, we propose Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding (PyPE), a novel approach designed to enhance the perception of visual tokens within VLMs. By assigning visual position indexes from the periphery to the center and expanding the central receptive field incrementally, PyPE addresses the limitations of traditional raster-scan methods and mitigates the long-term decay effects induced by Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). Our method reduces the relative distance between interrelated visual elements and instruction tokens, promoting a more rational allocation of attention weights and allowing for a multi-granularity perception of visual elements and countering the over-reliance on anchor tokens. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that PyPE consistently improves the general capabilities of VLMs across various sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/SakuraTroyChen/PyPE.

papers.title: Uncovering Layer-Dependent Activation Sparsity Patterns in ReLU Transformers
papers.research_question: How does token-level sparsity evolve over training in ReLU Transformers, and how do sparsity patterns differ across layers and between token, sequence, and batch levels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparsity patterns in ReLU Transformers are layer-dependent, with the first and last layers exhibiting inverted sparsity behaviors, and that neuron death is driven by training dynamics rather than random outliers.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity in ReLU Transformers varies systematically across layers, with the first and last layers being inverses in sparsity behavior, and that one can prune a significant fraction of hidden units without affecting accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Different layers in a ReLU Transformer exhibit distinct sparsity patterns, with the first layer using few hidden units per batch but using them frequently, and the last layer using many hidden units per batch but infrequently per token.
Sparsity patterns at token, sequence, and batch levels often anticorrelate, with layers that use few hidden units per token using many over a batch.
Neuron death (hidden units that never activate) is driven by training dynamics and occurs in specific regimes, rather than randomly.
A significant fraction of hidden units (about 5%) are never used from initialization, suggesting potential for better initialization methods.
Pruning hidden units that are never used after a point in training does not harm model performance, indicating potential for compute savings.
papers.limitation: The study focuses exclusively on small models and ReLU activation functions, which limits immediate applicability to modern foundation models.
future_direction: Investigate changes to initialization functions or model structure to allow more effective use of capacity in both ReLU and more competitive activation functions.
Study the underlying similarities in features learned between ReLU and smoothly-activated networks.
papers.abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that MLPs within ReLU Transformers exhibit high levels of sparsity, with many of their activations equal to zero for any given token. We build on that work to more deeply explore how token-level sparsity evolves over the course of training, and how it connects to broader sparsity patterns over the course of a sequence or batch, demonstrating that the different layers within small transformers exhibit distinctly layer-specific patterns on both of these fronts. In particular, we demonstrate that the first and last layer of the network have distinctive and in many ways inverted relationships to sparsity, and explore implications for the structure of feature representations being learned at different depths of the model. We additionally explore the phenomenon of ReLU dimensions "turning off", and show evidence suggesting that "neuron death" is being primarily driven by the dynamics of training, rather than simply occurring randomly or accidentally as a result of outliers.

papers.title: Fresh in memory: Training-order recency is linearly encoded in language model activations
papers.research_question: Do language models linearly encode when information was learned during training? Specifically, is training-order recency encoded in model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models linearly encode training-order recency in their activations, and this encoding is robust, generalizable, and accessible to the model itself.
papers.conclusion: Models linearly encode training-order information in their activations, a finding with significant implications for how models might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation centroids for test data from six sequential fine-tuning stages lie on a straight line in a 2D subspace, ordered exactly by training recency.
Linear probes can distinguish entities from the earliest and latest training stages with >90% accuracy, generalizing to held-out entities.
The encoding tracks recency: re-exposing a dataset moves its centroid to the 'most recent' position, and additional training on a stage pushes its centroid further.
The model can be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage with ~80% accuracy.
The encoding is not explained by simple activation statistics (norms, moments), output confidence, or geometric properties like PCA directions.
papers.limitation:
The persistence of the training-order signal through mixed-data training complicates a straightforward interpretation that the axis solely tracks exposure recency.
The signal for individual training datapoints (as opposed to entities) is weaker (~60% accuracy) and vanishes after mixed training, suggesting a different mechanism.
future_direction: Exploring whether fine-tuning access can be used to extract information about the order of pretraining data.
Finding a more precise interpretation of the training-order signal that accounts for its persistence through mixed-data training.
papers.abstract: We show that language models' activations linearly encode when information was learned during training. Our setup involves creating a model with a known training order by sequentially fine-tuning Llama-3.2-1B on six disjoint but otherwise similar datasets about named entities. We find that the average activations of test samples corresponding to the six training datasets encode the training order: when projected into a 2D subspace, these centroids are arranged exactly in the order of training and lie on a straight line. Further, we show that linear probes can accurately (~90%) distinguish "early" vs. "late" entities, generalizing to entities unseen during the probes' own training. The model can also be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage (~80% accuracy). Interestingly, the training-order encoding does not seem attributable to simple differences in activation magnitudes, losses, or model confidence. Our paper demonstrates that models are capable of differentiating information by its acquisition time, and carries significant implications for how they might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.

papers.title: Clustering units in neural networks: upstream vs downstream information
papers.research_question: How can we define and quantify modularity in neural networks? The paper investigates this by comparing upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity between hidden units.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that dropout increases modularity by making hidden units redundant, and that upstream and downstream definitions of functional similarity yield different clusters, indicating a misalignment between input-driven and output-driven neural representations.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that upstream and downstream ways of thinking about neural representations are not necessarily aligned, which has implications for representation learning and the definition of modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout dramatically increases modularity, contrary to the initial hypothesis that it would decrease modularity.
L2 regularization also increases modularity, while L1 regularization has a more modest effect.
Upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity agree within their families but disagree across families, leading to different cluster assignments.
The redundancy-inducing effect of dropout increases the clusterability of units.
Training increases cluster-similarity among upstream methods but not downstream methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to feedforward networks on MNIST, which may not have a meaningful modular solution.
Pairwise independence does not guarantee groupwise independence, which could be a limitation of the method.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks trained on more structured data, and to recurrent networks.
Evaluating the effect of maximizing modularity during training to see if it leads to performance benefits.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that some form of "modular" structure in artificial neural networks should be useful for learning, compositionality, and generalization. However, defining and quantifying modularity remains an open problem. We cast the problem of detecting functional modules into the problem of detecting clusters of similar-functioning units. This begs the question of what makes two units functionally similar. For this, we consider two broad families of methods: those that define similarity based on how units respond to structured variations in inputs ("upstream"), and those based on how variations in hidden unit activations affect outputs ("downstream"). We conduct an empirical study quantifying modularity of hidden layer representations of simple feedforward, fully connected networks, across a range of hyperparameters. For each model, we quantify pairwise associations between hidden units in each layer using a variety of both upstream and downstream measures, then cluster them by maximizing their "modularity score" using established tools from network science. We find two surprising results: first, dropout dramatically increased modularity, while other forms of weight regularization had more modest effects. Second, although we observe that there is usually good agreement about clusters within both upstream methods and downstream methods, there is little agreement about the cluster assignments across these two families of methods. This has important implications for representation-learning, as it suggests that finding modular representations that reflect structure in inputs (e.g. disentanglement) may be a distinct goal from learning modular representations that reflect structure in outputs (e.g. compositionality).

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
papers.research_question: Does attention provide a faithful explanation for model decisions by identifying important input components?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not reliably interpretable as importance indicators; they are only noisy predictors of input components' importance to the model.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not an optimal method of identifying which attended elements are responsible for an output; as an importance ranking, it fails to explain model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
The highest attention weight often has a larger impact than a random weight, but there are many cases where the impact is similar.
Attention weights often fail to identify the minimal set of representations that are important for the model's decision.
Gradient-based rankings of attention weights often predict their effects better than their magnitudes.
The scope of contextualization (e.g., RNN vs. convolutional encoders) affects how well attention indicates importance.
In encoderless models, attention magnitudes are more helpful, but still not optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on text classification, which may not generalize to tasks with larger output spaces (e.g., language modeling).
Reliance on argmax decision flips as a measure of importance, which might be too coarse.
Only evaluated on specific attention functions (additive attention) and final layers; other variants and lower layers might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other tasks and models with larger output spaces.
Develop better, more informative importance rankings.
Align models with human feedback for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have recently boosted performance on a range of NLP tasks. Because attention layers explicitly weight input components' representations, it is also often assumed that attention can be used to identify information that models found important (e.g., specific contextualized word tokens). We test whether that assumption holds by manipulating attention weights in already-trained text classification models and analyzing the resulting differences in their predictions. While we observe some ways in which higher attention weights correlate with greater impact on model predictions, we also find many ways in which this does not hold, i.e., where gradient-based rankings of attention weights better predict their effects than their magnitudes. We conclude that while attention noisily predicts input components' overall importance to a model, it is by no means a fail-safe indicator. 1

papers.title: Clustering Head: A Visual Case Study of the Training Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn the sparse modular addition task, and what are the training dynamics and circuit structures that emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a visual sandbox to study training dynamics of transformers on the sparse modular addition task, revealing clustering head circuits that capture task invariants and analyzing two-phase learning and loss spikes.
papers.conclusion: The visual sandbox provides insights into transformer training dynamics and circuit formation, offering a foundation for understanding larger models and guiding practical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Introduces the sparse modular addition problem and a visual sandbox for visualizing transformer training dynamics.
Unveils clustering heads, circuits that learn the task's invariants (permutation and suffix invariance).
Observes a two-phase learning process: first clustering sequence embeddings, then fitting the MLP classifier.
Identifies loss spikes caused by high curvature in normalization layers and feedforward networks.
Shows that successful models tend to have denser activations and discusses the effects of initialization and curriculum learning.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on a small transformer with a synthetic task, which may not directly generalize to large-scale models and real-world tasks.
future_direction: Apply the visual sandbox to larger models and more complex tasks.
Investigate smoothing normalization layers to mitigate loss spikes.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the sparse modular addition task and examines how transformers learn it. We focus on transformers with embeddings in $\R^2$ and introduce a visual sandbox that provides comprehensive visualizations of each layer throughout the training process. We reveal a type of circuit, called "clustering heads," which learns the problem's invariants. We analyze the training dynamics of these circuits, highlighting two-stage learning, loss spikes due to high curvature or normalization layers, and the effects of initialization and curriculum learning.

papers.title: Easing Optimization Paths: a Circuit Perspective
papers.research_question: How does gradient descent interact with circuits in neural networks, and how can this perspective be used to design curricula for efficient learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using a circuit perspective to understand neural network training dynamics, demonstrating that gradient descent reinforces useful circuits and prunes others, and that curriculum learning can ease optimization by fostering sub-circuits.
papers.conclusion: The circuit perspective provides valuable insights into training dynamics and can be used to design curricula for efficient learning, with potential for advancing deep learning both practically and theoretically.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent reinforces useful circuits while pruning non-invariant ones during training.
Networks break down complex tasks into sub-circuits for intermediate reasoning steps.
Curriculum learning helps in discovering generalizing circuits by first learning simpler sub-tasks.
There is a loss barrier between memorizing and generalizing solutions, which curriculum learning helps overcome.
Visualization of attention dynamics shows how spurious circuits are pruned over time.
future_direction: Study the interplay between gradient norms, loss spikes, and training stability using a circuit perspective.
Study the impact of activation sparsity on models’ performance using a circuit perspective.
papers.abstract: Gradient descent is the method of choice for training large artificial intelligence systems. As these systems become larger, a better understanding of the mechanisms behind gradient training would allow us to alleviate compute costs and help steer these systems away from harmful behaviors. To that end, we suggest utilizing the circuit perspective brought forward by mechanistic interpretability. After laying out our intuition, we illustrate how it enables us to design a curriculum for efficient learning in a controlled setting. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/pal}.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs): Visual Explainability of Learned Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we discover and visualize learned concepts in neural network layers by analyzing activation patterns beyond individual neuron analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs), a method for layer-level concept discovery in neural networks by clustering activation profiles, providing a visual explainability tool.
papers.conclusion: NAPs provide a layer-level explainability method that complements existing techniques, enabling deeper understanding of neural network models through visual introspection of learned concepts.
papers.key_findings:
NAPs can reveal distinct concepts learned at different layers, such as low-level features in early layers and high-level concepts in later layers.
NAPs allow for comparison of concepts across different models, revealing architectural differences and performance variations.
NAPs can uncover biases in training data, such as overrepresentation of certain contexts (e.g., people holding fish).
The method is robust across various network architectures and datasets, from simple MNIST models to complex ImageNet models.
NAPs complement existing unit-level explainability methods by providing layer-level insights.
papers.limitation:
NAPs require human interpretation and may not always reflect what the model sees.
The discovery of NAPs depends on the input data used; if a concept is not present in the input data, it cannot be extracted.
Earlier layers tend to produce fewer and less interpretable NAPs because they represent low-level features.
future_direction: Applying NAPs to different data types and tasks, such as GANs, Transformers, and RNNs.
Combining NAPs with attribution methods to highlight input features representative of a NAP.
Slicing activations across different dimensions, such as classes, to find intra-class differences.
papers.abstract: A key to deciphering the inner workings of neural networks is understanding what a model has learned. Promising methods for discovering learned features are based on analyzing activation values, whereby current techniques focus on analyzing high activation values to reveal interesting features on a neuron level. However, analyzing high activation values limits layer-level concept discovery. We present a method that instead takes into account the entire activation distribution. By extracting similar activation profiles within the high-dimensional activation space of a neural network layer, we find groups of inputs that are treated similarly. These input groups represent neural activation patterns (NAPs) and can be used to visualize and interpret learned layer concepts. We release a framework with which NAPs can be extracted from pre-trained models and provide a visual introspection tool that can be used to analyze NAPs. We tested our method with a variety of networks and show how it complements existing methods for analyzing neural network activation values.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
Cholinergic modulation is a common mechanism that biases processing toward external modes across multiple systems.
future_direction: Test the prediction that disruption of mode-switching (e.g., between non-REM and REM sleep) impairs integration of new hippocampal memories with existing neocortical knowledge.
Investigate how altering the timescale of switching affects the learning of temporally extended features.
Explore the role of neuromodulators like acetylcholine in regulating mode-switching and learning across different brain systems.
papers.abstract: Brains construct internal models that support perception, prediction, and action in the external world. Individual circuits within a brain also learn internal models of the local world of input they receive, in order to facilitate efficient and robust representation. How are these internal models learned? We propose that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing. We review computational evidence that this mode-switching can produce an error signal to drive learning. We then consider empirical evidence for the instantiation of mode-switching in diverse neural systems, ranging from subsecond fluctuations in the hippocampus to wake-sleep alternations across the whole brain. We hypothesize that these internal/external switching processes, which occur at multiple scales, can drive learning at each scale. This framework predicts that (a) slower mode-switching should be associated with learning of more temporally extended input features and (b) disruption of switching should impair the integration of new information with prior information.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads in multi-head attention models, and can a large percentage be pruned at test time without significantly impacting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Many attention heads in trained multi-head attention models are redundant and can be pruned without significant performance loss, with encoder-decoder attention being more reliant on multiple heads than self-attention.
papers.conclusion: Multi-head attention does not always fully leverage its theoretical expressiveness, and pruning heads can improve inference efficiency without harming performance, offering insights for more parameter-efficient models.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention heads can be individually removed at test time without a statistically significant drop in performance.
Some entire attention layers can be reduced to a single head without impacting performance.
A greedy pruning algorithm based on a gradient-derived importance score can remove 20-40% of heads without noticeable performance degradation.
Encoder-decoder attention layers are much more sensitive to pruning than self-attention layers.
The distinction between important and unimportant heads increases as training progresses, suggesting training dynamics play a role.
future_direction: A more principled investigation of the training dynamics of head importance.
Inspiring models that invest their parameters and attention more efficiently.
papers.abstract: Attention is a powerful and ubiquitous mechanism for allowing neural models to focus on particular salient pieces of information by taking their weighted average when making predictions. In particular, multi-headed attention is a driving force behind many recent state-of-the-art NLP models such as Transformer-based MT models and BERT. These models apply multiple attention mechanisms in parallel, with each attention "head" potentially focusing on different parts of the input, which makes it possible to express sophisticated functions beyond the simple weighted average. In this paper we make the surprising observation that even if models have been trained using multiple heads, in practice, a large percentage of attention heads can be removed at test time without significantly impacting performance. In fact, some layers can even be reduced to a single head. We further examine greedy algorithms for pruning down models, and the potential speed, memory efficiency, and accuracy improvements obtainable therefrom. Finally, we analyze the results with respect to which parts of the model are more reliant on having multiple heads, and provide precursory evidence that training dynamics play a role in the gains provided by multi-head attention.

papers.title: Abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained to perform multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How do abstract (disentangled) representations emerge in neural networks? The paper investigates whether training on multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge.
papers.core_contribution: Training neural networks on multiple tasks causes abstract (disentangled) representations to emerge, which enables few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: Abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and could be pervasive in high-level brain regions.
papers.key_findings:
Abstract representations emerge when the number of tasks (P) exceeds the number of latent variables (D).
These representations are robust to task heterogeneity, including unbalanced tasks, contextual tasks, and partial information.
Abstract representations emerge with both supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
The multi-tasking model produces abstract representations from image inputs (2D shapes and 3D chairs).
Abstract representations enable few-sample learning and generalization to novel tasks.
future_direction: Test the predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly in neural data.
Investigate abstract representations in more complex neural network architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract Humans and other animals demonstrate a remarkable ability to generalize knowledge across distinct contexts and objects during natural behavior. We posit that this ability to generalize arises from a specific representational geometry, that we call abstract and that is referred to as disentangled in machine learning. These abstract representations have been observed in recent neurophysiological studies. However, it is unknown how they emerge. Here, using feedforward neural networks, we demonstrate that the learning of multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge, using both supervised and reinforcement learning. We show that these abstract representations enable few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks. We conclude that abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and, as a consequence, could be pervasive in high-level brain regions. We also make several specific predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly.

papers.title: Peer Review #3 of "Learning to perform role-filler binding with schematic knowledge (v0.2)"
papers.core_contribution: Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) can learn to perform role-filler binding without explicit labels and generalize to arbitrary fillers, even those that violate training correlations, by storing bindings in their external memory components.
papers.conclusion: Networks with external memory can learn role-filler binding, a key component for learning flexible, structured cognitive representations, by extracting relations from input structure rather than relying on training correlations.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) learn to perform role-filler binding without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs.
These networks can generalize to previously unseen fillers when trained with an unlimited pool of fillers (Unlimited Filler Training).
The Fast Weights network shows biases towards statistical regularities from training, while the DNC does not, suggesting different binding mechanisms.
Decoding analyses indicate successful networks store role-filler bindings in their external memory components (fast weights matrix or memory buffer), not in the controller's hidden state.
Networks fail when test stories are presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training, indicating reliance on structural similarities.
papers.limitation:
Networks fail when given stories presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training.
The study does not prove that all standard RNN and LSTM models are unable to solve these tasks; future work with larger LSTMs might succeed.
future_direction: Training regimes that use shuffled stories during training to make models robust to test stories with shuffled segments.
Investigating how much a pool of train fillers needs to be expanded to allow networks to learn a representation that extends to previously unseen fillers.
Testing models of role-filler binding against neural data, potentially using paradigms for probing activity-silent memory.
papers.abstract: Through specific experiences, humans learn the relationships that underlie the structure of events in the world. Schema theory suggests that we organize this information in mental frameworks called "schemata," which represent our knowledge of the structure of the world. Generalizing knowledge of structural relationships to new situations requires rolefiller binding, the ability to associate specific "fillers" with abstract "roles." For instance, when we hear the sentence "Alice ordered a tea from Bob," the role-filler bindings "Alice:customer," "tea:drink," and "Bob:barista" allow us to understand and make inferences about the sentence. We can perform these bindings for arbitrary fillers -we understand this sentence even if we have never heard the names "Alice," "tea," or "Bob" before. In this work, we define a model as capable of performing role-filler binding if it can recall arbitrary fillers corresponding to a specified role, even when these pairings violate correlations seen during training. Previous work found that models can learn this ability when explicitly told what the roles and fillers are, or when given fillers seen during training. We show that networks with external memory learn to bind roles to arbitrary fillers, without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs. We further show that they can perform these bindings on role-filler pairs that violate correlations seen during training, while retaining knowledge of training correlations. We apply analyses inspired by neural decoding to interpret what the networks have learned.

papers.title: Counterfactual Divergence Singularity: A Theoretical Model of High-Similarity Instability and Micro-Counterfactual Drift in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the relationship between input similarity and output divergence in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations be formalized, and what explains the instability near high similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS), a theoretical framework that characterizes instability in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations, showing that divergence increases sharply as semantic similarity approaches unity.
papers.conclusion: The Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS) captures instability in LLMs under micro-counterfactual perturbations, reframing challenges like hallucination as manifestations of local non-smoothness in semantic manifolds, and suggests new evaluation paradigms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Divergence exhibits a hyperbolic blow-up as semantic similarity approaches 1.
Semantic curvature increases logarithmically in high-similarity regimes.
Embedding drift is minimal for high-similarity pairs, but divergence is high, indicating a contradiction.
LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth, leading to instability near the identity boundary.
The CDS phenomenon provides a geometric explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Scale and computational constraints with only 200 micro-counterfactual pairs.
Dependency on a single paraphraser (FLAN-T5-Base).
Dependence on a single embedding model (SBERT MiniLM-L6-v2).
Absence of output-level probability divergence analysis.
Limited to English-language textual inputs.
Interpretational boundaries, not claiming CDS explains all hallucinations.
future_direction: Scaling to larger datasets (e.g., 2,000–20,000 pairs).
Testing with different paraphrasers and embedding models.
Including output-level probability divergence analysis.
Extending to other languages and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable fluency and contextual sensitivity, yet their behaviour under minimal semantic perturbations remains poorly understood. In particular, near-identical paraphrastic inputs—expected to yield stable and equivalent responses—often produce disproportionately divergent generative behaviour. This paper introduces the <bold>Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS)</bold> , a theoretical and empirical framework that characterizes a previously underexplored instability regime in transformer-based language models. This work formalizes micro-counterfactual perturbations as infinitesimal semantic variations in embedding space and show that, as semantic similarity approaches unity, divergence metrics exhibit a hyperbolic blow-up. Using a controlled experimental pipeline based on FLAN-T5-generated paraphrases and Sentence-BERT semantic embeddings, this paper empirically demonstrate that divergence, curvature, and embedding drift collectively reveal a singular boundary where semantic proximity no longer guarantees behavioural stability. Despite minimal embedding displacement and near-maximal cosine similarity, reciprocal divergence measures increase sharply, exposing a structural nonlinearity in the input–output mapping of LLMs. The results suggest that LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth and that standard embedding-based similarity metrics fail to capture instability near the identity boundary. This phenomenon provides a geometric and mathematical explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and certain forms of hallucination observed in generative systems. By reframing these behaviours as consequences of latent-space singularities rather than isolated decoding artifacts, this work contributes a novel theoretical lens for evaluating robustness, interpretability, and reliability in large language models.

papers.title: Word Order Matters When You Increase Masking
papers.research_question: To what extent do masked language models require explicit position encoding to perform well on the masked language modeling objective, and how does the amount of masking affect this requirement?
papers.core_contribution: The utility of explicit position encoding in masked language models increases with the number of masked tokens; without position encoding, models cannot reconstruct position information when masking is high.
papers.conclusion: Position encoding becomes necessary for masked language modeling as the amount of masking increases, and the amount of masking should be carefully chosen to encourage models to use position information.
papers.key_findings:
When only one token is masked, models with and without position encoding perform similarly.
As the number of masked tokens increases, the true probability distribution for ordered contexts diverges from that of unordered contexts.
Models with position encoding (BERT) approximate the ordered distribution well, while models without (NP) approximate the unordered distribution.
The amount of masking is a crucial parameter for models to use position information.
papers.limitation:
The results are obtained on artificial languages, and adapting the method to natural languages may be difficult because the true probability distribution is not accessible.
Training multiple models on natural languages is computationally expensive.
The artificial language has fixed word order, so the findings may not generalize to natural languages with more flexible word order.
future_direction: Find proxies to estimate reference points for natural languages.
Evaluate impact of position encoding in languages with variable word order.
papers.abstract: Word order, an essential property of natural languages, is injected in Transformer-based neural language models using position encoding. However, recent experiments have shown that explicit position encoding is not always useful, since some models without such feature managed to achieve state-of-the art performance on some tasks. To understand better this phenomenon, we examine the effect of removing position encodings on the pre-training objective itself (i.e., masked language modelling), to test whether models can reconstruct position information from co-occurrences alone. We do so by controlling the amount of masked tokens in the input sentence, as a proxy to affect the importance of position information for the task. We find that the necessity of position information increases with the amount of masking, and that masked language models without position encodings are not able to reconstruct this information on the task. These findings point towards a direct relationship between the amount of masking and the ability of Transformers to capture order-sensitive aspects of language using position encoding.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Emergent Low-Rank Training Dynamics in MLPs with Smooth Activations
papers.research_question: How do training dynamics in MLPs with smooth activations concentrate within low-dimensional subspaces, and can this be leveraged for low-rank parameterization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that weight dynamics in MLPs with smooth activations concentrate in low-dimensional subspaces, theoretically characterizes these subspaces for two-layer networks, and proposes a low-rank MLP parameterization that matches full-rank performance with proper initialization.
papers.conclusion: Training dynamics of MLPs with smooth activations are low-dimensional, enabling effective low-rank parameterizations that match full-rank performance with proper initialization.
papers.key_findings:
For MLPs with smooth activations, weight updates are concentrated in low-dimensional subspaces that depend on initialization.
Theoretically, for two-layer networks, gradient updates are mostly in a rank-2K subspace.
Empirically, the phenomenon extends to deeper networks, different optimizers, and unwhitened data.
A low-rank MLP parameterization with proper initialization can match full-rank performance on classification tasks.
Initialization of the low-rank factors is crucial; random initialization leads to poor performance.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis assumes whitened input data, fixed second layer, and small initialization scale.
Theoretical results are limited to two-layer networks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other architectures and activation functions
Design efficient low-rank training algorithms
papers.abstract: Recent empirical evidence has demonstrated that the training dynamics of large-scale deep neural networks occur within low-dimensional subspaces. While this has inspired new research into low-rank training, compression, and adaptation, theoretical justification for these dynamics in nonlinear networks remains limited. %compared to deep linear settings. To address this gap, this paper analyzes the learning dynamics of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) under gradient descent (GD). We demonstrate that the weight dynamics concentrate within invariant low-dimensional subspaces throughout training. Theoretically, we precisely characterize these invariant subspaces for two-layer networks with smooth nonlinear activations, providing insight into their emergence. Experimentally, we validate that this phenomenon extends beyond our theoretical assumptions. Leveraging these insights, we empirically show there exists a low-rank MLP parameterization that, when initialized within the appropriate subspaces, matches the classification performance of fully-parameterized counterparts on a variety of classification tasks.

papers.title: Identifying Equivalent Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we identify equivalent training dynamics in deep neural networks? The paper proposes using topological conjugacy and Koopman operator theory to address this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Koopman operator theory-based framework to identify topologically conjugate training dynamics in deep neural networks, enabling the comparison of training dynamics across architectures and hyperparameters.
papers.conclusion: The Koopman-based framework is flexible and can shed new light on training dynamics across a range of DNN architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The framework correctly identifies the known topological conjugacy between online mirror descent and online gradient descent.
Narrow and wide fully connected neural networks exhibit non-conjugate training dynamics.
Different random initializations of wide FCNs can lead to conjugate training dynamics.
Convolutional neural networks show early training dynamics transitions, but LeNet and ResNet-20 have non-conjugate dynamics.
Transformers that undergo grokking and those that do not have non-conjugate training dynamics.
papers.limitation:
Numerical approximations of Koopman mode decomposition are only approximations and are subject to hyperparameter selection, choice of observable functions, and number of modes considered.
Assessing whether Koopman eigenvalues are sufficiently similar to indicate conjugacy is challenging; the Wasserstein distance and randomized shuffle control have limitations.
future_direction: Data-driven discovery and generation of new classes of optimization algorithms.
Learning mappings that transform one DNN model to another.
Characterizing Koopman eigenvalues across a wide range of DNN models to improve training methods.
papers.abstract: Study of the nonlinear evolution deep neural network (DNN) parameters undergo during training has uncovered regimes of distinct dynamical behavior. While a detailed understanding of these phenomena has the potential to advance improvements in training efficiency and robustness, the lack of methods for identifying when DNN models have equivalent dynamics limits the insight that can be gained from prior work. Topological conjugacy, a notion from dynamical systems theory, provides a precise definition of dynamical equivalence, offering a possible route to address this need. However, topological conjugacies have historically been challenging to compute. By leveraging advances in Koopman operator theory, we develop a framework for identifying conjugate and non-conjugate training dynamics. To validate our approach, we demonstrate that comparing Koopman eigenvalues can correctly identify a known equivalence between online mirror descent and online gradient descent. We then utilize our approach to: (a) identify non-conjugate training dynamics between shallow and wide fully connected neural networks; (b) characterize the early phase of training dynamics in convolutional neural networks; (c) uncover non-conjugate training dynamics in Transformers that do and do not undergo grokking. Our results, across a range of DNN architectures, illustrate the flexibility of our framework and highlight its potential for shedding new light on training dynamics.

papers.title: On the Cone Effect in the Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) evolve during neural network training, and what are the characteristics of the learning dynamics in real-world settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'cone effect' in the late-phase learning dynamics of neural networks, where the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) continues to evolve but within a constrained function space, providing significant performance advantages over the fully linearized (lazy) training regime.
papers.conclusion: The work unveils a cone effect in the late learning dynamics of neural networks, where the eNTK evolves in a constrained space during Phase II, offering performance advantages over the lazy regime, though this phenomenon is not universal.
papers.key_findings:
The learning dynamics exhibit a two-phase process: Phase I with significant eNTK evolution (rich regime) and Phase II where the eNTK evolves within a constrained space (cone effect).
The cone effect in Phase II provides non-negligible performance benefits over training solely in the lazy regime, as shown by a switching experiment from standard to linearized training.
The two-phase hypothesis and cone effect are not universal, as a counterexample (LeNet on MNIST) shows continuous kernel evolution without a clear two-phase pattern.
papers.limitation: The cone effect and two-phase hypothesis are not universal, as demonstrated by a counterexample (LeNet on MNIST) where the kernel keeps evolving without a clear two-phase pattern.
future_direction: Further efforts on uncovering the contributing factors of the cone effect are expected.
papers.abstract: Understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks is a central topic in the deep learning community. In this paper, we take an empirical perspective to study the learning dynamics of neural networks in real-world settings. Specifically, we investigate the evolution process of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) during training. Our key findings reveal a two-phase learning process: i) in Phase I, the eNTK evolves significantly, signaling the rich regime, and ii) in Phase II, the eNTK keeps evolving but is constrained in a narrow space, a phenomenon we term the cone effect. This two-phase framework builds on the hypothesis proposed by Fort et al. (2020), but we uniquely identify the cone effect in Phase II, demonstrating its significant performance advantages over fully linearized training.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction.
