Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: On the geometry of generalization and memorization in deep neural\n networks
papers.research_question: How does memorization of training data occur across the layers of a deep neural network, and what is the connection between the geometry of internal representations and generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization in deep neural networks occurs predominantly in the deeper layers due to decreasing manifold radius and dimension, while early layers learn general features; generalization can be restored by rewinding the final few layers' weights to an earlier epoch.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals the layer-wise structure of memorization in deep networks, showing it is concentrated in deeper layers and driven by geometric properties of representations, and links the double descent phenomenon to manifold geometry.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization occurs abruptly in the deeper layers of the network, while early layers learn general features that are minimally affected by label noise.
The geometry of object manifolds (capacity, radius, dimension) changes with depth and training time, and these geometric properties are linked to memorization and generalization.
Generalization performance can be largely restored by rewinding the parameters of the final few layers to an earlier epoch before significant memorization occurred.
The double descent phenomenon in generalization with increasing model size is linked to a non-monotonic change in the dimensionality of the object manifolds.
Gradient analysis shows that early in training, the gradient contribution from permuted (noise) examples is small, causing the network to initially ignore noise and learn shared features.
papers.abstract:
Understanding how large neural networks avoid memorizing training data is key
to explaining their high generalization performance. To examine the structure
of when and where memorization occurs in a deep network, we use a recently
developed replica-based mean field theoretic geometric analysis method. We find
that all layers preferentially learn from examples which share features, and
link this behavior to generalization performance. Memorization predominately
occurs in the deeper layers, due to decreasing object manifolds' radius and
dimension, whereas early layers are minimally affected. This predicts that
generalization can be restored by reverting the final few layer weights to
earlier epochs before significant memorization occurred, which is confirmed by
the experiments. Additionally, by studying generalization under different model
sizes, we reveal the connection between the double descent phenomenon and the
underlying model geometry. Finally, analytical analysis shows that networks
avoid memorization early in training because close to initialization, the
gradient contribution from permuted examples are small. These findings provide
quantitative evidence for the structure of memorization across layers of a deep
neural network, the drivers for such structure, and its connection to manifold
geometric properties.

papers.title: Contribution of task-irrelevant stimuli to drift of neural representations
papers.research_question: How do task-irrelevant stimuli contribute to representational drift in neural networks during online learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that task-irrelevant stimuli act as a source of noise in online learning, causing representational drift in neural networks across various architectures and learning rules.
papers.conclusion: The study links the structure of stimuli, task, and learning rule to representational drift, providing a theoretical foundation for using drift as a signal to uncover underlying computation in neural systems.
papers.key_findings:
Drift rate increases with the variance and dimension of task-irrelevant stimuli.
This phenomenon holds for Hebbian-based learning (Oja's rule, Similarity Matching) and stochastic gradient descent (autoencoder, two-layer network).
Drift due to learning noise has different geometric and dimension-dependency predictions than drift caused by Gaussian synaptic noise.
In MNIST data, drift rate peaks at an intermediate bottleneck dimension due to trade-off between representational space and noise from task-irrelevant stimuli.
Nonlinear networks with localized receptive fields also exhibit increased drift with task-irrelevant variance.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical derivations are limited to linear networks.
The framework assumes small learning rates and fluctuations around the solution.
The study does not consider task-irrelevant stimuli appearing in separate contexts.
future_direction: Future experiments controlling the amount of task-irrelevant stimuli to test predictions.
Extending the theory to nonlinear networks and large learning rates.
Investigating drift in contexts where task-irrelevant stimuli appear separately.
papers.abstract: Biological and artificial learners are inherently exposed to a stream of data and experience throughout their lifetimes and must constantly adapt to, learn from, or selectively ignore the ongoing input. Recent findings reveal that, even when the performance remains stable, the underlying neural representations can change gradually over time, a phenomenon known as representational drift. Studying the different sources of data and noise that may contribute to drift is essential for understanding lifelong learning in neural systems. However, a systematic study of drift across architectures and learning rules, and the connection to task, are missing. Here, in an online learning setup, we characterize drift as a function of data distribution, and specifically show that the learning noise induced by task-irrelevant stimuli, which the agent learns to ignore in a given context, can create long-term drift in the representation of task-relevant stimuli. Using theory and simulations, we demonstrate this phenomenon both in Hebbian-based learning -- Oja's rule and Similarity Matching -- and in stochastic gradient descent applied to autoencoders and a supervised two-layer network. We consistently observe that the drift rate increases with the variance and the dimension of the data in the task-irrelevant subspace. We further show that this yields different qualitative predictions for the geometry and dimension-dependency of drift than those arising from Gaussian synaptic noise. Overall, our study links the structure of stimuli, task, and learning rule to representational drift and could pave the way for using drift as a signal for uncovering underlying computation in the brain.

papers.title: Hypernym Bias: Unraveling Deep Classifier Training Dynamics through the Lens of Class Hierarchy
papers.research_question: What patterns do neural networks learn first and last? Specifically, how do hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Networks learn hypernyms (higher-level categories) earlier than hyponyms (specific categories) during training, and we introduce a framework to track this hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Hypernym bias is a consistent phenomenon across architectures and datasets, providing a framework for studying training dynamics and connecting early training bias to neural collapse.
papers.key_findings:
Hypernyms reach near maximum recognition accuracy early in training.
The learned representations align with the semantic structure of the dataset (WordNet).
Neural collapse properties appear earlier in hypernym label spaces.
The phenomenon is consistent across architectures (ResNet, ViT, MobileNet) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, DBPedia).
The training dynamics can be interpreted as top-to-bottom hierarchical label clustering.
papers.limitation:
The hierarchical structure of WordNet is imperfect and may not fully capture class relationships.
The phenomenon is less pronounced in datasets with less defined hierarchies (e.g., CIFAR-100).
future_direction: Extend the notion of hypernym bias to other domains (e.g., AudioSet).
Learn class hierarchies through data-driven hierarchical clustering instead of relying on external structures.
Investigate theoretical connections between hypernym bias and other known biases (e.g., simplicity bias, frequency principle).
papers.abstract: We investigate the training dynamics of deep classifiers by examining how hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training. Through extensive experiments, we argue that the learning process in classification problems can be understood through the lens of label clustering. Specifically, we observe that networks tend to distinguish higher-level (hypernym) categories in the early stages of training, and learn more specific (hyponym) categories later. We introduce a novel framework to track the evolution of the feature manifold during training, revealing how the hierarchy of class relations emerges and refines across the network layers. Our analysis demonstrates that the learned representations closely align with the semantic structure of the dataset, providing a quantitative description of the clustering process. Notably, we show that in the hypernym label space, certain properties of neural collapse appear earlier than in the hyponym label space, helping to bridge the gap between the initial and terminal phases of learning. We believe our findings offer new insights into the mechanisms driving hierarchical learning in deep networks, paving the way for future advancements in understanding deep learning dynamics.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Studying the Evolution of Neural Activation Patterns During Training of Feed-Forward ReLU Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural activation patterns evolve during training for different network architectures and training strategies? Specifically, the paper investigates the retention of initialization information, the order and timing of structural convergence, the evolution of functional expressivity, and the confirmation of known early-training dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a technique to efficiently record activation statistics (e.g., entropy, pattern similarity) during training and uses it to analyze the evolution of activation patterns in ReLU networks, revealing architecture- and method-specific behavioral patterns.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of activation patterns provides new insights into the discrete optimization process during neural network training, connecting architectural and training method choices to the resulting changes in network structure and expressivity.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns change most rapidly in the early phase of training, with many patterns from initialization being replaced quickly.
Residual networks (ResNets) retain a higher proportion of activation patterns from initialization compared to networks without skip connections.
Activation entropy (a measure of expressivity) typically drops after the first few training steps and then recovers, with architecture-specific curves; ResNets maintain higher expressivity.
PyramidNet and ResNet with FixUp initialization show more uniform convergence of activation patterns across layers, in contrast to the bottom-up convergence seen in conventional CNNs.
The distribution of activation patterns confirms known observations about the early phase of training, such as rapid changes and the impact of unfavorable batches.
papers.abstract: The ability of deep neural networks to form powerful emergent representations of complex statistical patterns in data is as remarkable as imperfectly understood. For deep ReLU networks, these are encoded in the mixed discrete-continuous structure of linear weight matrices and non-linear binary activations. Our article develops a new technique for instrumenting such networks to efficiently record activation statistics, such as information content (entropy) and similarity of patterns, in real-world training runs. We then study the evolution of activation patterns during training for networks of different architecture using different training and initialization strategies. As a result, we see characteristic- and general-related as well as architecture-related behavioral patterns: in particular, most architectures form bottom-up structure, with the exception of highly tuned state-of-the-art architectures and methods (PyramidNet and FixUp), where layers appear to converge more simultaneously. We also observe intermediate dips in entropy in conventional CNNs that are not visible in residual networks. A reference implementation is provided under a free license.

papers.title: Interpreting Recurrent and Attention-Based Neural Models: a Case Study on Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the intermediate layers (attention and LSTM gating signals) of neural models for Natural Language Inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces saliency-based visualization methods for interpreting attention and LSTM gating signals in neural models for Natural Language Inference, revealing insights into model decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization and interpretation strategies for neural models provide insights into how and why they work, demonstrating effectiveness on the complex NLI task.
papers.key_findings:
Attention saliency maps highlight which word alignments critically contribute to the model's prediction, whereas standard attention visualizations do not.
Comparing models via attention saliency reveals differences in focus; ESIM-300 correctly attends to gender connections while ESIM-50 does not.
Saliency patterns of LSTM gating signals differ across examples and can identify sentence parts important for the model's decision.
The inference LSTM shows more concentrated saliency on key sentence parts compared to the more spread-out saliency in the input LSTM.
Forward and backward LSTMs provide complementary understanding, sometimes focusing on different parts of the sentence.
future_direction: Extend the study to other NLP tasks and models to produce useful insights for further improving these models.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in natural language inference (NLI) tasks. While these models are widely explored, they are hard to interpret and it is often unclear how and why they actually work. In this paper, we take a step toward explaining such deep learning based models through a case study on a popular neural model for NLI.

papers.title: Detecting Learning vs Memorization in Deep Neural Networks using Shared Structure Validation Sets
papers.research_question: How can we differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained with real labels, as opposed to shuffled labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel permutation approach using shared structure validation sets (s-validation sets) and shallow classifiers to differentiate between learning and memorization in DNNs trained with real labels.
papers.conclusion: The proposed permutation approach using s-validation sets provides a useful tool for understanding how DNNs memorize and learn over training epochs.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs can simultaneously learn and memorize during training.
Regularization (e.g., dropout) and increasing the number of layers can reduce memorization.
DNNs exhibit dynamic memorization patterns over training epochs, with an initial memorization phase followed by a forgetting phase.
Surprisingly, DNNs can learn from pure Gaussian noise inputs, not just memorize them.
The method is useful for relative comparisons of memorization between different DNNs, but not for absolute quantification.
papers.limitation: The method cannot quantify the absolute amount of memorization in a DNN, only relative comparisons between models.
papers.abstract: The roles played by learning and memorization represent an important topic in deep learning research. Recent work on this subject has shown that the optimization behavior of DNNs trained on shuffled labels is qualitatively different from DNNs trained with real labels. Here, we propose a novel permutation approach that can differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained as usual (i.e., using the real labels to guide the learning, rather than shuffled labels). The evaluation of weather the DNN has learned and/or memorized, happens in a separate step where we compare the predictive performance of a shallow classifier trained with the features learned by the DNN, against multiple instances of the same classifier, trained on the same input, but using shuffled labels as outputs. By evaluating these shallow classifiers in validation sets that share structure with the training set, we are able to tell apart learning from memorization. Application of our permutation approach to multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks trained on image data corroborated many findings from other groups. Most importantly, our illustrations also uncovered interesting dynamic patterns about how DNNs memorize over increasing numbers of training epochs, and support the surprising result that DNNs are still able to learn, rather than only memorize, when trained with pure Gaussian noise as input.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Predicate learning in neural systems: Discovering latent generative structures
papers.research_question: How can latent representational structures (predicates) be learned from experience with unstructured data in neural systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains how predicate learning enables neural systems to discover latent generative structures from unstructured data using intersective comparison and neural oscillations, supporting compositionality and human-like generalization.
papers.conclusion: Predicate learning demonstrates how symbolic structures can be learned from neural signals, linking computational principles to neurophysiology and enabling complex human-like behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Predicate learning uses intersective comparison to detect invariants and form latent structures from unstructured data.
Neural oscillations, specifically desynchronization, enable dynamic binding of predicates and arguments without altering their meanings.
This approach allows for compositionality through rhythmic computation, facilitating the generation of new representations.
Predicate learning supports extrapolatory generalization to unseen data, as demonstrated in video game tasks.
It bridges symbolic representations and neural computation, offering insights into human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Humans learn complex latent structures from their environments (e.g., natural language, mathematics, music, social hierarchies). In cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience, models that infer higher-order structures from sensory or first-order representations have been proposed to account for the complexity and flexibility of human behavior. But how do the structures that these models invoke arise in neural systems in the first place? To answer this question, we explain how a system can learn latent representational structures (i.e., predicates) from experience with wholly unstructured data. During the process of predicate learning, an artificial neural network exploits the naturally occurring dynamic properties of distributed computing across neuronal assemblies in order to learn predicates, but also to combine them compositionally, two computational aspects which appear to be necessary for human behavior as per formal theories in multiple domains. We describe how predicates can be combined generatively using neural oscillations to achieve human-like extrapolation and compositionality in an artificial neural network. The ability to learn predicates from experience, to represent structures compositionally, and to extrapolate to unseen data offers an inroads to understanding and modeling the most complex human behaviors.

papers.title: Meta-Learning Neural Mechanisms rather than Bayesian Priors
papers.research_question: What does meta-learning imbue models with? Does it learn simplicity-based priors or neural mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (e.g., counters) into models, rather than learning simplicity-based priors, providing efficient meta-learning paradigms and theoretical insights linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Meta-trained models do not mimic the statistical properties of their meta-training dataset; instead, they acquire useful neural mechanisms, and meta-training on mechanistically-complex languages is vital for encouraging such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Models meta-trained on simplicity-bias datasets do not outperform those on complexity-bias datasets, contradicting the simplicity-bias view.
Meta-training on a single formal language can be as effective as meta-training on 5000 different languages if the language incentivizes useful neural mechanisms.
Meta-training on context-free and context-sensitive languages outperforms meta-training on regular languages, indicating mechanistic complexity matters.
GRUs do not show the same meta-learning improvement as LSTMs, likely because they cannot acquire counting mechanisms.
The Chomsky hierarchy may not fully capture the neural mechanisms useful for a given architecture, suggesting need for alternative hierarchies.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to formal language learning and does not look at more complicated domains like natural language.
The work does not explicitly examine hidden layers to find the presence of neural counters.
future_direction: Investigate alternative theoretical hierarchies that correspond to neural mechanisms useful in specific architectures.
Explore meta-learning in different architectures beyond LSTMs and GRUs, such as Transformers or Stack-RNNs.
Develop computational hierarchies akin to the Chomsky hierarchy but defined in terms of neural architectures and their mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Children acquire language despite being exposed to several orders of magnitude less data than large language models require. Meta-learning has been proposed as a way to integrate human-like learning biases into neural-network architectures, combining both the structured generalizations of symbolic models with the scalability of neural-network models. But what does meta-learning exactly imbue the model with? We investigate the meta-learning of formal languages and find that, contrary to previous claims, meta-trained models are not learning simplicity-based priors when meta-trained on datasets organised around simplicity. Rather, we find evidence that meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (such as counters) into the model, which function like cognitive primitives for the network on downstream tasks. Most surprisingly, we find that meta-training on a single formal language can provide as much improvement to a model as meta-training on 5000 different formal languages, provided that the formal language incentivizes the learning of useful neural mechanisms. Taken together, our findings provide practical implications for efficient meta-learning paradigms and new theoretical insights into linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.

papers.title: The Underlying Correlated Dynamics in Neural Training
papers.research_question: Can the dynamics of neural network parameters during training be modeled by grouping parameters into highly correlated modes, and does this representation reduce dimensionality and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Correlation Mode Decomposition (CMD), a method to model neural network training dynamics by clustering parameters into highly correlated groups (modes), which dramatically reduces dimensionality and can induce regularization for better generalization.
papers.conclusion: CMD is an effective method for modeling neural network training dynamics, reducing dimensionality, and improving generalization, paving the way for better network analysis and acceleration techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters during training can be grouped into a few highly correlated modes, providing a low-dimensional representation of the dynamics.
CMD induces regularization, leading to more stable training and improved test performance compared to original gradient descent.
CMD is robust to the number of modes and the sampling of weights for clustering.
CMD outperforms Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) in modeling training dynamics, especially with augmentations and complex architectures.
The typical time profiles of modes are spread throughout the network across all layers.
papers.limitation: CMD is applied post-training and requires checkpointing at each epoch, which can be memory-consuming for large models.
future_direction: Using CMD for network analysis and designing acceleration techniques.
papers.abstract: Training of neural networks is a computationally intensive task. The significance of understanding and modeling the training dynamics is growing as increasingly larger networks are being trained. We propose in this work a model based on the correlation of the parameters' dynamics, which dramatically reduces the dimensionality. We refer to our algorithm as \emph{correlation mode decomposition} (CMD). It splits the parameter space into groups of parameters (modes) which behave in a highly correlated manner through the epochs. We achieve a remarkable dimensionality reduction with this approach, where networks like ResNet-18, transformers and GANs, containing millions of parameters, can be modeled well using just a few modes. We observe each typical time profile of a mode is spread throughout the network in all layers. Moreover, our model induces regularization which yields better generalization capacity on the test set. This representation enhances the understanding of the underlying training dynamics and can pave the way for designing better acceleration techniques.

papers.title: Better Pre-Training by Reducing Representation Confusion
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to reduce two types of information confusion in pre-trained language models: confusion between distance and direction in relative position encoding, and high similarity between token representations and between head representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two techniques to reduce information confusion in pre-training: DDRP encoding decouples distance and direction in relative position encoding, and MTH objective reduces similarity between token and head representations, leading to improved performance and faster pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reducing information confusion in representation learning through DDRP and MTH improves pre-trained language models, and suggests broader applications of this principle.
papers.key_findings:
DDRP outperforms classical relative position encoding (BERT-R) and other baselines (TUPE, DEBERTA) on GLUE tasks without additional computational overhead.
MTH outperforms MLM by 0.96 average GLUE score and achieves nearly 2x pre-training speedup on BERTBASE.
DDRP reduces the number of parameters for relative position encoding from 2*rs to rs+3.
MTH reduces the average cosine self-similarity of token and head representations, leading to more discriminative representations.
DDRP exhibits a stronger directional bias in attention heads, with 92.11% of sentences showing an up-down triangle effect compared to 78.94% for BERT-R.
papers.limitation: The proposed methods induce additional computational costs: DDRP increases computational cost by about 5% compared to BERT, and MTH increases cost by about 4% compared to MLM.
future_direction: Exploring broader application scenarios for reducing information confusion in representation learning.
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the Transformer-based pre-trained language models and identify two different types of information confusion in position encoding and model representations, respectively. Firstly, we show that in the relative position encoding, the joint modeling about relative distances and directions brings confusion between two heterogeneous information. It may make the model unable to capture the associative semantics of the same distance and the opposite directions, which in turn affects the performance of downstream tasks. Secondly, we notice the BERT with Mask Language Modeling (MLM) pre-training objective outputs similar token representations (last hidden states of different tokens) and head representations (attention weightsof different heads), which may make the diversity of information expressed by different tokens and heads limited.Motivated by the above investigation, we propose two novel techniques to improve pre-trained language models: Decoupled Directional Relative Position (DDRP) encoding and MTH pre-training objective. DDRP decouples the relative distance features and the directional features in classical relative position encoding. MTH applies two novel auxiliary regularizers besides MLM to enlarge the dissimilarities between (a) last hidden states of different tokens, and (b) attention weights of different heads. These designs allow the model to capture different categories of information more clearly, as a way to alleviate information confusion in representation learning for better optimization.Extensive experiments and ablation studies on GLUE benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Lazy vs hasty: linearization in deep networks impacts learning schedule based on example difficulty
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effect of the lazy (linear) and feature learning (non-linear) regimes on the training dynamics of various groups of examples of increasing difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: In the feature learning (non-linear) regime, easy examples are given more weight and learned faster compared to difficult ones, leading to a sequential learning schedule based on example difficulty.
papers.conclusion: The non-linear (feature learning) regime prioritizes easy examples, resulting in a sequential learning schedule that can be beneficial for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Easy examples are learned faster in the non-linear regime compared to the linear regime.
The non-linear regime shows a more pronounced simplicity bias, prioritizing easy examples.
In the presence of label noise, the non-linear regime delays memorization of noisy examples, leading to better generalization.
In spurious correlation setups, the non-linear regime is more prone to learning the spurious feature initially.
Theoretical analysis in a quadratic model confirms that non-linearity induces sequential learning of modes based on their difficulty.
papers.abstract: Among attempts at giving a theoretical account of the success of deep neural networks, a recent line of work has identified a so-called lazy training regime in which the network can be well approximated by its linearization around initialization. Here we investigate the comparative effect of the lazy (linear) and feature learning (non-linear) regimes on subgroups of examples based on their difficulty. Specifically, we show that easier examples are given more weight in feature learning mode, resulting in faster training compared to more difficult ones. In other words, the non-linear dynamics tends to sequentialize the learning of examples of increasing difficulty. We illustrate this phenomenon across different ways to quantify example difficulty, including c-score, label noise, and in the presence of easy-to-learn spurious correlations. Our results reveal a new understanding of how deep networks prioritize resources across example difficulty.

papers.title: Higher Embedding Dimension Creates a Stronger World Model for a Simple Sorting Task
papers.research_question: How does embedding dimension affect the emergence of an internal world model in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps?
papers.core_contribution: Higher embedding dimensions lead to more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations (world models) in transformers trained on a sorting task, even after task accuracy saturates at lower dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build simple, structured internal world models even in constrained reinforcement learning settings, and increased model capacity (embedding dimension) improves the quality of these internal representations beyond what is reflected by task accuracy alone.
papers.key_findings:
The last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of input tokens.
The chosen adjacent swap corresponds to the largest difference between consecutive values in the encoded global ordering.
Task accuracy saturates at relatively low embedding dimensions (around 6 for length 6 sequences), but the fidelity and robustness of the internal ordering representation continue to improve up to around dimension 30.
Higher embedding dimensions make the learned internal mechanisms more consistent across different training runs and random seeds.
Low-dimension agents can fall into a 'local greedy trap', failing to form a coherent global ordering representation, a failure mode that decreases with higher embedding dimensions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited in scope and scale, focusing only on adjacent transposition sorting with 1-2 layer, single-head transformers, and does not explore more complex architectures or richer environments.
Computational budget restricted the ability to test broader ranges of sequence lengths or larger training runs.
future_direction: Relax the adjacency constraint to allow arbitrary in-place swaps to see if transformers discover known efficient algorithms or novel heuristics.
Introduce stochasticity into the environment (e.g., noisy token values or partial observability) to test if the ordering circuit emerges under uncertainty.
Explore hybrid training setups (e.g., supervised pre-training on optimal swaps followed by RL fine-tuning) to see if the ordering representation becomes more robust.
Introduce multi-head attention to examine if different heads specialize in complementary subproblems.
Test the robustness of the identified circuits under pruning or quantization, and apply similar analyses to structurally richer algorithmic tasks (e.g., graph algorithms).
papers.abstract: We investigate how embedding dimension affects the emergence of an internal "world model" in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps. Models achieve high accuracy even with very small embedding dimensions, but larger dimensions yield more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations. In particular, higher embedding dimensions strengthen the formation of structured internal representation and lead to better interpretability. After hundreds of experiments, we observe two consistent mechanisms: (1) the last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of tokens; and (2) the selected transposition aligns with the largest adjacent difference of these encoded values. Our results provide quantitative evidence that transformers build structured internal world models and that model size improves representation quality in addition to end performance. We release our metrics and analyses, which can be used to probe similar algorithmic tasks.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Anatomy of Catastrophic Forgetting: Hidden Representations and Task Semantics
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting affect the hidden representations of neural networks, and how is it influenced by task semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that catastrophic forgetting is primarily driven by changes in deeper layers, and that forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in higher layers, mitigation methods stabilize these layers, and forgetting is maximized for tasks of intermediate similarity, providing a foundation for understanding and mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper layers are the primary source of forgetting in neural networks.
Forgetting mitigation methods like elastic weight consolidation and replay buffers act by stabilizing deeper layer representations.
Forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
Representational similarity (measured by CKA) between tasks is key to understanding forgetting.
A novel CIFAR-100 distribution shift task approximates realistic input distribution shift for studying forgetting.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in developing versatile machine learning systems is catastrophic forgetting: a model trained on tasks in sequence will suffer significant performance drops on earlier tasks. Despite the ubiquity of catastrophic forgetting, there is limited understanding of the underlying process and its causes. In this paper, we address this important knowledge gap, investigating how forgetting affects representations in neural network models. Through representational analysis techniques, we find that deeper layers are disproportionately the source of forgetting. Supporting this, a study of methods to mitigate forgetting illustrates that they act to stabilize deeper layers. These insights enable the development of an analytic argument and empirical picture relating the degree of forgetting to representational similarity between tasks. Consistent with this picture, we observe maximal forgetting occurs for task sequences with intermediate similarity. We perform empirical studies on the standard split CIFAR-10 setup and also introduce a novel CIFAR-100 based task approximating realistic input distribution shift.

papers.title: Adding Interpretable Attention to Neural Translation Models Improves Word Alignment
papers.research_question: How can high-accuracy word alignments be extracted from the activations of a state-of-the-art neural machine translation model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a simple extension to the Transformer architecture (an alignment layer) and a novel inference procedure using stochastic gradient descent to optimize attention activations, enabling unsupervised extraction of word alignments comparable to statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method of extending the Transformer with an alignment layer and using SGD-based attention optimization can extract meaningful word alignments in an unsupervised manner, achieving quality comparable to IBM Model 4 (Giza++) on two out of three tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an alignment layer to the Transformer decoder, which lacks skip connections and is forced to rely on encoder information, significantly improves word alignment quality over naively averaging attention activations.
Optimizing the attention activations via stochastic gradient descent to maximize the likelihood of the target word further improves alignment quality.
The proposed method achieves alignment error rates comparable to Giza++ on German-English and Romanian-English datasets.
The neural alignment models benefit more from symmetrizing bidirectional alignments than statistical methods, possibly due to using full source context but not full target context.
Using a combination of word embeddings and encoder output as the key/value representation in the alignment layer yields the best results.
papers.limitation: The method does not outperform Giza++ on the English-French dataset, which the authors attribute to the large portion of 'probable' alignment links in the reference set, which favors Giza++'s tendency to predict fewer alignments.
papers.abstract: Multi-layer models with multiple attention heads per layer provide superior translation quality compared to simpler and shallower models, but determining what source context is most relevant to each target word is more challenging as a result. Therefore, deriving high-accuracy word alignments from the activations of a state-of-the-art neural machine translation model is an open challenge. We propose a simple model extension to the Transformer architecture that makes use of its hidden representations and is restricted to attend solely on encoder information to predict the next word. It can be trained on bilingual data without word-alignment information. We further introduce a novel alignment inference procedure which applies stochastic gradient descent to directly optimize the attention activations towards a given target word. The resulting alignments dramatically outperform the naive approach to interpreting Transformer attention activations, and are comparable to Giza++ on two publicly available data sets.

papers.title: Luck Matters: Understanding Training Dynamics of Deep ReLU Networks
papers.research_question: How does training dynamics of deep ReLU networks lead to generalization, and how can it explain phenomena like over-parameterization, implicit regularization, and lottery tickets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework for training dynamics of deep ReLU networks in a teacher-student setting, showing that lucky nodes close to teacher nodes converge faster and irrelevant nodes' fan-out weights vanish, explaining phenomena like over-parameterization and lottery tickets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a theoretical framework that explains training dynamics of deep ReLU networks and provides insight into several empirical phenomena, with future work to extend the analysis to more general settings.
papers.key_findings:
Student nodes whose weights are initialized close to teacher nodes converge to them at a faster rate.
In over-parameterized regimes, a small set of lucky nodes converge to teacher nodes while the fan-out weights of other nodes converge to zero.
The framework explains multiple puzzling phenomena: over-parameterization, implicit regularization, lottery tickets, flat minima, and fitting both structured and random data.
BatchNorm biases in pre-trained VGG models are mostly negative, supporting the assumption of small overlapping teacher node activations.
Experiments on Gaussian data and CIFAR-10 validate the theoretical predictions.
papers.limitation:
Theorem 5 is limited to 2-layer networks; extension to multi-layer is future work.
Assumption 3 (small overlap between teacher nodes) may not always hold.
Finite datasets cause convergence to stall, unlike infinite data.
future_direction: Extend Theorem 5 to general multi-layer setting
Relax Assumption 3
Study more BatchNorm effects
papers.abstract: We analyze the dynamics of training deep ReLU networks and their implications on generalization capability. Using a teacher-student setting, we discovered a novel relationship between the gradient received by hidden student nodes and the activations of teacher nodes for deep ReLU networks. With this relationship and the assumption of small overlapping teacher node activations, we prove that (1) student nodes whose weights are initialized to be close to teacher nodes converge to them at a faster rate, and (2) in over-parameterized regimes and 2-layer case, while a small set of lucky nodes do converge to the teacher nodes, the fan-out weights of other nodes converge to zero. This framework provides insight into multiple puzzling phenomena in deep learning like over-parameterization, implicit regularization, lottery tickets, etc. We verify our assumption by showing that the majority of BatchNorm biases of pre-trained VGG11/16 models are negative. Experiments on (1) random deep teacher networks with Gaussian inputs, (2) teacher network pre-trained on CIFAR-10 and (3) extensive ablation studies validate our multiple theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: Dynamic Position Encoding for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be improved by dynamically encoding target position information to enhance translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Position Encoding (DPE), a novel method that generates embeddings containing target word position information to improve neural machine translation in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: DPE consistently outperforms baselines by helping the source side learn target position information, demonstrating the usefulness of dynamic position encoding in Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
DPE improves BLEU scores over the baseline Transformer Base and other position encoding methods.
The improvement is due to the injection of position information, not just additional parameters, as shown by comparisons with increased encoder layers.
DPE is effective across different language pairs and dataset sizes, including IWSLT-14 and WMT-14.
Ablation studies show that the position loss weight λ=0.5 provides the best balance for translation accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The alignment tool FastAlign may not handle all cases like Many-to-Many alignments and multi-word expressions perfectly.
Limited investment in linguistic preprocessing due to resource constraints.
future_direction: Design additional rules for handling different word alignment cases.
Investigate more precise alignment tools beyond FastAlign.
Explore injecting order information into other language processing models like dependency parsing or sequence tagging.
papers.abstract: Recurrent models have been dominating the field of neural machine translation (NMT) for the past few years. Transformers \citep{vaswani2017attention}, have radically changed it by proposing a novel architecture that relies on a feed-forward backbone and self-attention mechanism. Although Transformers are powerful, they could fail to properly encode sequential/positional information due to their non-recurrent nature. To solve this problem, position embeddings are defined exclusively for each time step to enrich word information. However, such embeddings are fixed after training regardless of the task and the word ordering system of the source or target language. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture with new position embeddings depending on the input text to address this shortcoming by taking the order of target words into consideration. Instead of using predefined position embeddings, our solution generates new embeddings to refine each word's position information. Since we do not dictate the position of source tokens and learn them in an end-to-end fashion, we refer to our method as dynamic position encoding (DPE). We evaluated the impact of our model on multiple datasets to translate from English into German, French, and Italian and observed meaningful improvements in comparison to the original Transformer.

papers.title: Visualizing the PHATE of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the internal geometry and learning dynamics of neural networks to understand why certain networks outperform others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces M-PHATE, a visualization method that reveals the internal geometry and learning dynamics of neural networks by capturing the evolution of hidden unit activations over training, providing insights into phenomena like catastrophic forgetting and generalization without needing validation data.
papers.conclusion: M-PHATE provides an interpretable visualization of neural network learning dynamics, offering unique insights into network performance and behavior that are not apparent from classical metrics like validation loss and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, showing rapid structural changes and crossing of unit trajectories when tasks switch.
Increased heterogeneity among hidden units in M-PHATE visualizations correlates with improved generalization performance, while networks that memorize (e.g., with random labels) show low heterogeneity.
M-PHATE outperforms standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., t-SNE, Isomap) in capturing both the dynamics and community structure of hidden units during training.
The method allows meaningful comparison of hidden units across different layers, as neurons from different layers frequently co-localize in the visualization.
M-PHATE can be applied using only training data, providing a way to understand generalization performance without access to a validation set.
papers.abstract: Understanding why and how certain neural networks outperform others is key to guiding future development of network architectures and optimization methods. To this end, we introduce a novel visualization algorithm that reveals the internal geometry of such networks: Multislice PHATE (M-PHATE), the first method designed explicitly to visualize how a neural network's hidden representations of data evolve throughout the course of training. We demonstrate that our visualization provides intuitive, detailed summaries of the learning dynamics beyond simple global measures (i.e., validation loss and accuracy), without the need to access validation data. Furthermore, M-PHATE better captures both the dynamics and community structure of the hidden units as compared to visualization based on standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., ISOMAP, t-SNE). We demonstrate M-PHATE with two vignettes: continual learning and generalization. In the former, the M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of "catastrophic forgetting" which is a major challenge for learning in task-switching contexts. In the latter, our visualizations reveal how increased heterogeneity among hidden units correlates with improved generalization performance. An implementation of M-PHATE, along with scripts to reproduce the figures in this paper, is available at https://github.com/scottgigante/M-PHATE.

papers.title: Attention Guided CAM: Visual Explanations of Vision Transformer Guided by Self-Attention
papers.research_question: How to provide a high-level semantic explanation for Vision Transformer's decisions with great localization performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided gradient analysis method for Vision Transformer that provides high-level semantic explanations with great localization performance by combining gradients propagated from the classification output with self-attention scores normalized by sigmoid.
papers.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided gradient analysis method provides a reliable explanation of ViT and achieves state-of-the-art performance in weakly-supervised object localization, making ViT more adaptable to tasks involving object localization.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method outperforms previous leading explainability methods (Attention Rollout and LRP-based) for ViT in weakly-supervised localization tasks across multiple datasets.
The method reduces the peak intensity problem in visualization heatmaps by normalizing self-attention scores with sigmoid instead of softmax.
The method successfully captures the full area of target objects and multiple instances within an image, providing more precise and faithful explanations.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformer(ViT) is one of the most widely used models in the computer vision field with its great performance on various tasks. In order to fully utilize the ViT-based architecture in various applications, proper visualization methods with a decent localization performance are necessary, but these methods employed in CNN-based models are still not available in ViT due to its unique structure. In this work, we propose an attention-guided visualization method applied to ViT that provides a high-level semantic explanation for its decision. Our method selectively aggregates the gradients directly propagated from the classification output to each self-attention, collecting the contribution of image features extracted from each location of the input image. These gradients are additionally guided by the normalized self-attention scores, which are the pairwise patch correlation scores. They are used to supplement the gradients on the patch-level context information efficiently detected by the self-attention mechanism. This approach of our method provides elaborate high-level semantic explanations with great localization performance only with the class labels. As a result, our method outperforms the previous leading explainability methods of ViT in the weakly-supervised localization task and presents great capability in capturing the full instances of the target class object. Meanwhile, our method provides a visualization that faithfully explains the model, which is demonstrated in the perturbation comparison test.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: Deconstructing Positional Information: From Attention Logits to Training Biases
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding schemes (additive vs. multiplicative) mediate the interaction between token content and position, and what causes the performance paradox and single-head deposit pattern in RoPE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified Toeplitz-matrix framework to analyze positional encodings, discovers the single-head deposit pattern in RoPE, and provides a theoretical explanation showing this pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE's multiplicative structure.
papers.conclusion: The Toeplitz framework provides a powerful lens for understanding positional encodings, and the deposit pattern explains RoPE's performance paradox. Controlled mixing of positional signals is a promising strategy for achieving robust, distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's multiplicative structure enables superior performance on tasks requiring content-position coupling but leads to a single-head deposit pattern where positional information is concentrated in one early-layer head.
Additive positional encodings (Absolute, T5, ALiBi) do not exhibit the deposit pattern and show different learning dynamics.
The deposit pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE, caused by exponential amplification of gradient signals during training, leading to extreme specialization.
Hybrid architectures like Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) can mitigate the deposit pattern and improve robustness by mixing positional signals.
