papers.abstract: Over the past few years, an extensively studied phenomenon in training deep networks is the implicit bias of gradient descent towards parsimonious solutions. In this work, we investigate this phenomenon by narrowing our focus to deep linear networks. Through our analysis, we reveal a surprising "law of parsimony" in the learning dynamics when the data possesses low-dimensional structures. Specifically, we show that the evolution of gradient descent starting from orthogonal initialization only affects a minimal portion of singular vector spaces across all weight matrices. In other words, the learning process happens only within a small invariant subspace of each weight matrix, despite the fact that all weight parameters are updated throughout training. This simplicity in learning dynamics could have significant implications for both efficient training and a better understanding of deep networks. First, the analysis enables us to considerably improve training efficiency by taking advantage of the low-dimensional structure in learning dynamics. We can construct smaller, equivalent deep linear networks without sacrificing the benefits associated with the wider counterparts. Second, it allows us to better understand deep representation learning by elucidating the linear progressive separation and concentration of representations from shallow to deep layers. We also conduct numerical experiments to support our theoretical results. The code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/cjyaras/lawofparsimony.

papers.title: Word Order Does Matter and Shuffled Language Models Know It
papers.research_question: Do shuffled language models still have traces of word order information? Why is there a gap in performance between models without position embeddings and models trained on shuffled tokens? Are there NLU benchmarks, other than GLUE, on which shuffled language models perform poorly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models trained on shuffled text retain word order information due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and correlations between sentence length and content, and that some NLU tasks are sensitive to word order.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that models trained on shuffled text retain word order knowledge, largely at the local level, due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations. The order of shuffling (before/after BPE) influences this acquisition, and some NLU tasks are highly sensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled language models contain word order information, as shown by probing tasks.
The performance gap between models without position embeddings and shuffled models is due to position embeddings providing inductive bias and the presence of n-grams when shuffling before BPE segmentation.
Even when shuffling after segmentation, models retain some word order information due to statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities.
Attention patterns in shuffled models show a bias towards adjacent tokens.
Some NLU tasks (e.g., Winograd Schema, ReCoRD) require word order information and show significant performance drops for shuffled models.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models' good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain information pertaining to the original, naturalistic word order. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work -before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning. * Equal contribution. Order was decided by a coin toss.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Empirical influence functions to understand the logic of fine-tuning
papers.research_question: How do individual training samples affect model outputs during fine-tuning, and do the resulting influence functions obey desirable properties such as semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces empirical influence functions (EIFs) to analyze fine-tuning, revealing that fine-tuning violates key desiderata for learning (e.g., logical consistency, causality), while prompting can partially rescue these failures.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuned models do not learn in a way that respects logical and causal relationships; prompting is a better way to incorporate new knowledge, suggesting models may be more like lookup machines than reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical influence functions show fine-tuning does not obey desiderata like decreasing influence with semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency.
For CNNs, the influence matrix is symmetric and noise has no influence on how much the model relies on a sample.
For LLMs (Phi-3), the influence matrix is asymmetric but does not reflect desired inferential asymmetry (e.g., transitivity, ontology, causality).
Prompting (in-context learning) can partially rescue these failures, leading to more asymmetric and logical influence functions.
Influence functions are densely populated, meaning models use irrelevant data as much as relevant data.
papers.limitation:
The approach is relatively slow, requiring fine-tuning for each training sample and then inference for each test sample.
The linearity assumption (neural tangent kernel) may not hold for all models.
The desiderata are superficial and not grounded in deep linguistic understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to the entire training process of LLMs.
Building meta-learning systems that optimize influence functions to obey the desiderata.
Using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a strategy to ameliorate the violations.
papers.abstract: Understanding the process of learning in neural networks is crucial for improving their performance and interpreting their behavior. This can be approximately understood by asking how a model's output is influenced when we fine-tune on a new training sample. There are desiderata for such influences, such as decreasing influence with semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency. Here we use the empirical influence measured using fine-tuning to demonstrate how individual training samples affect outputs. We show that these desiderata are violated for both for simple convolutional networks and for a modern LLM. We also illustrate how prompting can partially rescue this failure. Our paper presents an efficient and practical way of quantifying how well neural networks learn from fine-tuning stimuli. Our results suggest that popular models cannot generalize or perform logic in the way they appear to.

papers.title: Phases of learning dynamics in artificial neural networks: with or without mislabeled data
papers.research_question: How can we understand the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) learning dynamics in artificial neural networks using a statistical physics framework, and what are the distinct phases of learning with and without mislabeled data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a statistical physics and stochastic dynamical systems framework to characterize SGD learning dynamics, identifying distinct phases of learning with and without mislabeled data, and shows how the separation of loss distributions in phase II enables a simple method to clean mislabeled data and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: The statistical physics and stochastic dynamical systems approach provides a useful theoretical framework for understanding SGD learning dynamics in neural networks, which may lead to more efficient learning algorithms and a deeper understanding of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Without mislabeled data, SGD learning dynamics transitions from a fast learning phase (directed motion with high gradient alignment) to a slow exploration phase (diffusive motion with low alignment).
With mislabeled data, SGD learning dynamics exhibits four phases: phase I (learning correctly labeled data), phase II (wandering with balanced gradients), phase III (learning mislabeled data), and phase IV (exploration after memorization).
Transitions between phases are characterized by changes in order parameters that measure the alignment and relative strength of gradients from correctly and incorrectly labeled datasets.
In phase II, the individual loss distributions for correctly and mislabeled samples are most separated, which can be used to identify and clean mislabeled samples.
A simple cleaning method based on loss separation in phase II significantly improves generalization performance for datasets with up to 80% labeling noise.
future_direction: Generalization and the double descent behavior
Relation between task complexity and network architecture
Information flow in deep neural networks
Transfer learning, curriculum learning, and continuous learning
papers.abstract: Despite tremendous success of deep neural network in machine learning, the underlying reason for its superior learning capability remains unclear. Here, we present a framework based on statistical physics to study dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) that drives learning in neural networks. By using the minibatch gradient ensemble, we construct order parameters to characterize dynamics of weight updates in SGD. Without mislabeled data, we find that the SGD learning dynamics transitions from a fast learning phase to a slow exploration phase, which is associated with large changes in order parameters that characterize the alignment of SGD gradients and their mean amplitude. In the case with randomly mislabeled samples, SGD learning dynamics falls into four distinct phases. The system first finds solutions for the correctly labeled samples in phase I, it then wanders around these solutions in phase II until it finds a direction to learn the mislabeled samples during phase III, after which it finds solutions that satisfy all training samples during phase IV. Correspondingly, the test error decreases during phase I and remains low during phase II; however, it increases during phase III and reaches a high plateau during phase IV. The transitions between different phases can be understood by changes of order parameters that characterize the alignment of mean gradients for the correctly and incorrectly labeled samples and their (relative) strength during learning. We find that individual sample losses for the two datasets are most separated during phase II, which leads to a cleaning process to eliminate mislabeled samples for improving generalization.

papers.title: New Evidence of the Two-Phase Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural network training dynamics exhibit a two-phase transition from chaotic exploration to stable refinement?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interval-wise analysis framework for neural network training dynamics and identifies two new phenomena, the Chaos Effect and Cone Effect, which reveal a structural two-phase transition from sensitive exploration to stable refinement.
papers.conclusion: The interval-wise analysis reveals a two-phase transition in neural network training dynamics, from an early chaotic, exploratory phase to a later stable, refinement phase constrained within a narrow functional cone.
papers.key_findings:
An inflection point emerges during training, marking a significant change in the direction of the optimization trajectory.
Tiny parameter perturbations applied before the inflection point lead to substantial divergence in later training, indicating a chaotic early regime (Chaos Effect).
After the inflection point, the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) evolves within a narrow, constrained region in function space (Cone Effect).
The Cone Effect provides significant performance advantages over purely linearized (lazy) training regimes.
papers.limitation:
The work is primarily empirical and lacks a thorough theoretical analysis.
Experiments are limited to image classification tasks (CIFAR-10).
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of the observed phenomena
Exploration of empirical evidence beyond image classification tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep neural networks learn remains a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning. A growing body of evidence suggests that training dynamics undergo a distinct phase transition, yet our understanding of this transition is still incomplete. In this paper, we introduce an interval-wise perspective that compares network states across a time window, revealing two new phenomena that illuminate the two-phase nature of deep learning. i) \textbf{The Chaos Effect.} By injecting an imperceptibly small parameter perturbation at various stages, we show that the response of the network to the perturbation exhibits a transition from chaotic to stable, suggesting there is an early critical period where the network is highly sensitive to initial conditions; ii) \textbf{The Cone Effect.} Tracking the evolution of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK), we find that after this transition point the model's functional trajectory is confined to a narrow cone-shaped subset: while the kernel continues to change, it gets trapped into a tight angular region. Together, these effects provide a structural, dynamical view of how deep networks transition from sensitive exploration to stable refinement during training.

papers.title: Consequences of Slow Neural Dynamics for Incremental Learning
papers.research_question: How does the temporal smoothness of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned?
papers.core_contribution: Networks with linear recurrence and gating learn more efficiently from temporally correlated data and can learn internal representations that separate fast and slow sources in the environment.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation is not an obstacle for learning but can be an inductive bias that accelerates learning and leads to more interpretable, timescale-separated representations when learning from correlated data streams.
papers.key_findings:
Feedforward networks learn slower with temporally autocorrelated data, while networks with linear recurrence learn faster.
Adding a gating mechanism to reset memory at category transitions allows recurrent networks to benefit from autocorrelation while avoiding interference from unrelated prior information.
Networks with recurrence and multiscale gating can learn internal representations that un-mix features varying on different timescales from multi-scale autocorrelated data.
The linear-recurrence-plus-gating model generalizes better across different levels of temporal autocorrelation compared to an LSTM trained with backpropagation through time.
Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation in neural dynamics can serve as a useful inductive bias for incremental learning from correlated data.
papers.limitation:
The gating mechanism in the autoencoder experiments is somewhat artificial as it requires knowing which features change quickly or slowly.
The work uses simple architectures and synthetic datasets; future work should test on larger architectures and more realistic datasets.
future_direction: Examine the efficacy of linear recurrence and gating mechanisms in CNN architectures trained on video segmentation sequences.
Test whether results generalize to larger architectures and more realistic datasets with a broader hyperparameter search.
Extend the autoencoder architecture to a predictive architecture that predicts the next stimulus rather than reconstructing the present one.
Investigate the broader consequences of learning with recurrence for reducing the difference between human internal representations and those of feedforward nets.
papers.abstract: In the human brain, internal states are often correlated over time (due to local recurrence and other intrinsic circuit properties), punctuated by abrupt transitions. At first glance, temporal smoothness of internal states presents a problem for learning input-output mappings (e.g. category labels for images), because the internal representation of the input will contain a mixture of current input and prior inputs. However, when training with naturalistic data (e.g. movies) there is also temporal autocorrelation in the input. How does the temporal "smoothness" of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned? We found that, when trained with temporally smooth data, "slow" neural networks (equipped with linear recurrence and gating mechanisms) learned to categorize more efficiently than feedforward networks. Furthermore, networks with linear recurrence and multi-timescale gating could learn internal representations that "un-mixed" quickly-varying and slowly-varying data sources. Together, these findings demonstrate how a fundamental property of cortical dynamics (their temporal autocorrelation) can serve as an inductive bias, leading to more efficient category learning and to the representational separation of fast and slow sources in the environment.

papers.title: Uncovering Memorization Effect in the Presence of Spurious Correlations
papers.research_question: Does memorization play a role in spurious correlations and imbalanced group performance in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spurious memorization, concentrated in a small subset of neurons, is a key driver of imbalanced group performance in the presence of spurious correlations, and proposes a fine-tuning framework to mitigate this effect.
papers.conclusion: Spurious memorization in a small subset of neurons is a fundamental cause of imbalanced group performance, and strategically disrupting this memorization can lead to more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of critical neurons is responsible for memorizing minority group examples during training.
Modifying (e.g., pruning, randomizing) these critical neurons significantly affects training accuracy on minority groups but has minimal impact on majority groups.
Both gradient-based and magnitude-based criteria can effectively identify these critical neurons.
Removing spurious memorization through a proposed fine-tuning framework improves worst-group test accuracy across different architectures and datasets.
The memorization of minority examples by a limited neuron subset leads to poor test robustness for those groups.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models often rely on simple spurious features -- patterns in training data that correlate with targets but are not causally related to them, like image backgrounds in foreground classification. This reliance typically leads to imbalanced test performance across minority and majority groups. In this work, we take a closer look at the fundamental cause of such imbalanced performance through the lens of memorization, which refers to the ability to predict accurately on atypical examples (minority groups) in the training set but failing in achieving the same accuracy in the testing set. This paper systematically shows the ubiquitous existence of spurious features in a small set of neurons within the network, providing the first-ever evidence that memorization may contribute to imbalanced group performance. Through three experimental sources of converging empirical evidence, we find the property of a small subset of neurons or channels in memorizing minority group information. Inspired by these findings, we hypothesize that spurious memorization, concentrated within a small subset of neurons, plays a key role in driving imbalanced group performance. To further substantiate this hypothesis, we show that eliminating these unnecessary spurious memorization patterns via a novel framework during training can significantly affect the model performance on minority groups. Our experimental results across various architectures and benchmarks offer new insights on how neural networks encode core and spurious knowledge, laying the groundwork for future research in demystifying robustness to spurious correlation.

papers.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
papers.research_question: Why do artifacts (high-norm tokens) appear in feature maps of vision transformers, and how can they be fixed?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies artifacts (high-norm tokens) in vision transformer feature maps and proposes a simple fix by adding register tokens to the input sequence, which removes artifacts and improves performance on dense prediction tasks and object discovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper exposes artifacts in vision transformer feature maps, proposes adding register tokens as a simple fix, and demonstrates its effectiveness across supervised, text-supervised, and self-supervised models.
papers.key_findings:
Artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens that appear primarily in low-informative background areas of images.
These high-norm tokens hold global image information but little local patch information.
Adding register tokens to the input sequence entirely removes the artifacts, leading to smoother feature and attention maps.
Models trained with register tokens show improved performance on dense prediction tasks like segmentation and depth estimation.
Register tokens enable object discovery methods (e.g., LOST) to work effectively with modern vision transformers.
papers.limitation: The authors have not been able to fully determine which aspects of the training led to the appearance of artifacts in different models.
future_direction: Study the regularization of registers.
Investigate why the value projection in OpenCLIP filters out outliers even without registers.
papers.abstract: Transformers have recently emerged as a powerful tool for learning visual representations. In this paper, we identify and characterize artifacts in feature maps of both supervised and self-supervised ViT networks. The artifacts correspond to high-norm tokens appearing during inference primarily in low-informative background areas of images, that are repurposed for internal computations. We propose a simple yet effective solution based on providing additional tokens to the input sequence of the Vision Transformer to fill that role. We show that this solution fixes that problem entirely for both supervised and self-supervised models, sets a new state of the art for self-supervised visual models on dense visual prediction tasks, enables object discovery methods with larger models, and most importantly leads to smoother feature maps and attention maps for downstream visual processing.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: The Early Phase of Neural Network Training
papers.research_question: What changes do deep neural networks undergo during the early phase of training, and how do these changes depend on data and labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the early phase of training involves structured changes in weight distributions that are not captured by signs alone, and that these changes can be approximated by self-supervised pre-training without labels, though labels accelerate the process.
papers.conclusion: The early phase of training is crucial for subsequent learning, and the changes are not simply due to noise but involve structured learning that can be achieved via self-supervised pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
The early phase of training consists of three sub-phases: initial large gradients and rapid motion, followed by gradient stabilization and rapid performance increase, and then deceleration.
Deeper networks are not robust to reinitialization with random weights while maintaining signs, contrary to findings in smaller networks.
Weight distributions after early training are highly non-i.i.d., as permuting them within layers or globally harms performance.
Pre-training with self-supervised tasks (e.g., rotation prediction) can approximate the changes from supervised training, but requires many more epochs (32x longer).
Labels are not necessary for the early phase changes, but they significantly accelerate the process; however, misleading labels (random labels) prevent these changes.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that many important aspects of neural network learning take place within the very earliest iterations or epochs of training. For example, sparse, trainable sub-networks emerge (Frankle et al., 2019), gradient descent moves into a small subspace (Gur-Ari et al., 2018), and the network undergoes a critical period (Achille et al., 2019). Here, we examine the changes that deep neural networks undergo during this early phase of training. We perform extensive measurements of the network state during these early iterations of training and leverage the framework of Frankle et al. (2019) to quantitatively probe the weight distribution and its reliance on various aspects of the dataset. We find that, within this framework, deep networks are not robust to reinitializing with random weights while maintaining signs, and that weight distributions are highly non-independent even after only a few hundred iterations. Despite this behavior, pre-training with blurred inputs or an auxiliary self-supervised task can approximate the changes in supervised networks, suggesting that these changes are not inherently label-dependent, though labels significantly accelerate this process. Together, these results help to elucidate the network changes occurring during this pivotal initial period of learning.

papers.title: Toward an Integration of Deep Learning and Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can principles from deep learning (cost function optimization, diverse cost functions, structured architectures) be used to understand the brain? Specifically, does the brain optimize cost functions, are these cost functions diverse and change over development, and do specialized brain systems enable efficient optimization for specific problem classes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes three hypotheses linking deep learning and neuroscience: (1) the brain optimizes cost functions, (2) cost functions are diverse across brain areas and change over development, and (3) specialized brain systems allow efficient solution of key computational problems.
papers.conclusion: Integrating deep learning and neuroscience provides a framework for understanding the brain as a heterogeneously optimized system, and the paper outlines future experimental directions to test the hypotheses.
future_direction: Experiments to identify cost functions in the brain
Investigations of credit assignment mechanisms in neural circuits
Studies of specialized brain systems and their computational roles
papers.abstract: Neuroscience has focused on the detailed implementation of computation, studying neural codes, dynamics and circuits. In machine learning, however, artificial neural networks tend to eschew precisely designed codes, dynamics or circuits in favor of brute force optimization of a cost function, often using simple and relatively uniform initial architectures. Two recent developments have emerged within machine learning that create an opportunity to connect these seemingly divergent perspectives. First, structured architectures are used, including dedicated systems for attention, recursion and various forms of short- and long-term memory storage. Second, cost functions and training procedures have become more complex and are varied across layers and over time. Here we think about the brain in terms of these ideas. We hypothesize that (1) the brain optimizes cost functions, (2) the cost functions are diverse and differ across brain locations and over development, and (3) optimization operates within a pre-structured architecture matched to the computational problems posed by behavior. In support of these hypotheses, we argue that a range of implementations of credit assignment through multiple layers of neurons are compatible with our current knowledge of neural circuitry, and that the brain's specialized systems can be interpreted as enabling efficient optimization for specific problem classes. Such a heterogeneously optimized system, enabled by a series of interacting cost functions, serves to make learning data-efficient and precisely targeted to the needs of the organism. We suggest directions by which neuroscience could seek to refine and test these hypotheses.

papers.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
papers.research_question: What are the distinct training dynamics and phase transitions that occur at small versus large learning rates in deep networks, and how do they affect generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the catapult mechanism, a dynamical phase transition in training dynamics that allows deep networks to stably train at large learning rates, leading to flatter minima and improved generalization.
papers.conclusion: The catapult mechanism enables training at large learning rates by reducing curvature, leading to flatter minima and improved generalization, thereby bridging infinite-width theory and practical deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies three learning rate phases: lazy (η < 2/λ0), catapult (2/λ0 < η < η_max), and divergent (η > η_max), with distinct training dynamics.
In the catapult phase, the loss initially grows (catapult effect) while curvature rapidly decreases, after which training converges to a flat minimum.
The catapult phase often yields optimal generalization performance, and the maximum learning rate η_max is approximately 12/λ0 for ReLU networks.
Theoretical analysis shows that the catapult dynamics are non-perturbative and cannot be captured by linearized models or finite-width perturbative expansions.
Empirical validation across various architectures (fully-connected, convolutional, Wide ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) confirms the predicted phases and performance trends.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to MSE loss; extension to softmax classification is not explored.
Behavior for other optimizers such as SGD with momentum may differ and is not studied.
The simple model predicts maximum learning rate 4/λ0, but for ReLU networks it is higher (≈12/λ0), indicating possible separate mechanisms.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to softmax classification.
Study the effect of optimizers such as SGD with momentum.
Investigate the reason for the higher maximum learning rate in ReLU networks.
papers.abstract: The choice of initial learning rate can have a profound effect on the performance of deep networks. We present a class of neural networks with solvable training dynamics, and confirm their predictions empirically in practical deep learning settings. The networks exhibit sharply distinct behaviors at small and large learning rates. The two regimes are separated by a phase transition. In the small learning rate phase, training can be understood using the existing theory of infinitely wide neural networks. At large learning rates the model captures qualitatively distinct phenomena, including the convergence of gradient descent dynamics to flatter minima. One key prediction of our model is a narrow range of large, stable learning rates. We find good agreement between our model's predictions and training dynamics in realistic deep learning settings. Furthermore, we find that the optimal performance in such settings is often found in the large learning rate phase. We believe our results shed light on characteristics of models trained at different learning rates. In particular, they fill a gap between existing wide neural network theory, and the nonlinear, large learning rate, training dynamics relevant to practice.

papers.title: Advancing General Multimodal Capability of Vision-language Models with Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding
papers.research_question: How does visual position encoding affect the perception capabilities of Vision-language Models (VLMs), and can a novel encoding method mitigate limitations like long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern' to improve multi-granularity perception?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding (PyPE), a novel position assignment strategy for visual tokens in VLMs that assigns indexes from periphery to center and incrementally expands the central receptive field, mitigating long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern' to improve multi-granularity perception and reduce hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: PyPE effectively addresses limitations of conventional visual position encoding methods by mitigating long-term decay and the 'aggregation pattern', leading to improved multi-granularity perception and overall performance of VLMs across diverse benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
PyPE consistently improves performance across various VQA and general multimodal benchmarks for VLMs of different sizes.
PyPE reduces object hallucinations and misunderstandings in generated descriptions compared to baseline position encoding methods.
The method alleviates the 'aggregation pattern' (over-reliance on anchor tokens) and enables more rational attention weight allocation.
PyPE demonstrates superior fine-grained perception while maintaining competitive coarse-grained perception capabilities.
A moderate descent interval (e.g., every 2 layers) generally provides the best balance of performance across tasks.
papers.limitation: PyPE is currently limited to single-frame images and has not yet been extended to video and other modalities.
future_direction: Effectively integrating the temporal dimension for unified position encoding in videos.
Extending PyPE to a broader range of VLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in advancing general artificial intelligence, yet the irrational encoding of visual positions persists in inhibiting the models' comprehensive perception performance across different levels of granularity. In this work, we propose Pyramid-descent Visual Position Encoding (PyPE), a novel approach designed to enhance the perception of visual tokens within VLMs. By assigning visual position indexes from the periphery to the center and expanding the central receptive field incrementally, PyPE addresses the limitations of traditional raster-scan methods and mitigates the long-term decay effects induced by Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). Our method reduces the relative distance between interrelated visual elements and instruction tokens, promoting a more rational allocation of attention weights and allowing for a multi-granularity perception of visual elements and countering the over-reliance on anchor tokens. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that PyPE consistently improves the general capabilities of VLMs across various sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/SakuraTroyChen/PyPE.

papers.title: Uncovering Layer-Dependent Activation Sparsity Patterns in ReLU Transformers
papers.research_question: How does token-level sparsity evolve over training in ReLU Transformers, and how do sparsity patterns differ across layers and between token, sequence, and batch levels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparsity patterns in ReLU Transformers are layer-dependent, with the first and last layers exhibiting inverted sparsity behaviors, and that neuron death is driven by training dynamics rather than random outliers.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity in ReLU Transformers varies systematically across layers, with the first and last layers being inverses in sparsity behavior, and that one can prune a significant fraction of hidden units without affecting accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Different layers in a ReLU Transformer exhibit distinct sparsity patterns, with the first layer using few hidden units per batch but using them frequently, and the last layer using many hidden units per batch but infrequently per token.
Sparsity patterns at token, sequence, and batch levels often anticorrelate, with layers that use few hidden units per token using many over a batch.
Neuron death (hidden units that never activate) is driven by training dynamics and occurs in specific regimes, rather than randomly.
A significant fraction of hidden units (about 5%) are never used from initialization, suggesting potential for better initialization methods.
Pruning hidden units that are never used after a point in training does not harm model performance, indicating potential for compute savings.
papers.limitation: The study focuses exclusively on small models and ReLU activation functions, which limits immediate applicability to modern foundation models.
future_direction: Investigate changes to initialization functions or model structure to allow more effective use of capacity in both ReLU and more competitive activation functions.
Study the underlying similarities in features learned between ReLU and smoothly-activated networks.
papers.abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that MLPs within ReLU Transformers exhibit high levels of sparsity, with many of their activations equal to zero for any given token. We build on that work to more deeply explore how token-level sparsity evolves over the course of training, and how it connects to broader sparsity patterns over the course of a sequence or batch, demonstrating that the different layers within small transformers exhibit distinctly layer-specific patterns on both of these fronts. In particular, we demonstrate that the first and last layer of the network have distinctive and in many ways inverted relationships to sparsity, and explore implications for the structure of feature representations being learned at different depths of the model. We additionally explore the phenomenon of ReLU dimensions "turning off", and show evidence suggesting that "neuron death" is being primarily driven by the dynamics of training, rather than simply occurring randomly or accidentally as a result of outliers.

papers.title: Fresh in memory: Training-order recency is linearly encoded in language model activations
papers.research_question: Do language models linearly encode when information was learned during training? Specifically, is training-order recency encoded in model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models linearly encode training-order recency in their activations, and this encoding is robust, generalizable, and accessible to the model itself.
papers.conclusion: Models linearly encode training-order information in their activations, a finding with significant implications for how models might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation centroids for test data from six sequential fine-tuning stages lie on a straight line in a 2D subspace, ordered exactly by training recency.
Linear probes can distinguish entities from the earliest and latest training stages with >90% accuracy, generalizing to held-out entities.
The encoding tracks recency: re-exposing a dataset moves its centroid to the 'most recent' position, and additional training on a stage pushes its centroid further.
The model can be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage with ~80% accuracy.
The encoding is not explained by simple activation statistics (norms, moments), output confidence, or geometric properties like PCA directions.
papers.limitation:
The persistence of the training-order signal through mixed-data training complicates a straightforward interpretation that the axis solely tracks exposure recency.
The signal for individual training datapoints (as opposed to entities) is weaker (~60% accuracy) and vanishes after mixed training, suggesting a different mechanism.
future_direction: Exploring whether fine-tuning access can be used to extract information about the order of pretraining data.
Finding a more precise interpretation of the training-order signal that accounts for its persistence through mixed-data training.
papers.abstract: We show that language models' activations linearly encode when information was learned during training. Our setup involves creating a model with a known training order by sequentially fine-tuning Llama-3.2-1B on six disjoint but otherwise similar datasets about named entities. We find that the average activations of test samples corresponding to the six training datasets encode the training order: when projected into a 2D subspace, these centroids are arranged exactly in the order of training and lie on a straight line. Further, we show that linear probes can accurately (~90%) distinguish "early" vs. "late" entities, generalizing to entities unseen during the probes' own training. The model can also be fine-tuned to explicitly report an unseen entity's training stage (~80% accuracy). Interestingly, the training-order encoding does not seem attributable to simple differences in activation magnitudes, losses, or model confidence. Our paper demonstrates that models are capable of differentiating information by its acquisition time, and carries significant implications for how they might manage conflicting data and respond to knowledge modifications.

papers.title: Clustering units in neural networks: upstream vs downstream information
papers.research_question: How can we define and quantify modularity in neural networks? The paper investigates this by comparing upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity between hidden units.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that dropout increases modularity by making hidden units redundant, and that upstream and downstream definitions of functional similarity yield different clusters, indicating a misalignment between input-driven and output-driven neural representations.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that upstream and downstream ways of thinking about neural representations are not necessarily aligned, which has implications for representation learning and the definition of modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout dramatically increases modularity, contrary to the initial hypothesis that it would decrease modularity.
L2 regularization also increases modularity, while L1 regularization has a more modest effect.
Upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity agree within their families but disagree across families, leading to different cluster assignments.
The redundancy-inducing effect of dropout increases the clusterability of units.
Training increases cluster-similarity among upstream methods but not downstream methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to feedforward networks on MNIST, which may not have a meaningful modular solution.
Pairwise independence does not guarantee groupwise independence, which could be a limitation of the method.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks trained on more structured data, and to recurrent networks.
Evaluating the effect of maximizing modularity during training to see if it leads to performance benefits.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that some form of "modular" structure in artificial neural networks should be useful for learning, compositionality, and generalization. However, defining and quantifying modularity remains an open problem. We cast the problem of detecting functional modules into the problem of detecting clusters of similar-functioning units. This begs the question of what makes two units functionally similar. For this, we consider two broad families of methods: those that define similarity based on how units respond to structured variations in inputs ("upstream"), and those based on how variations in hidden unit activations affect outputs ("downstream"). We conduct an empirical study quantifying modularity of hidden layer representations of simple feedforward, fully connected networks, across a range of hyperparameters. For each model, we quantify pairwise associations between hidden units in each layer using a variety of both upstream and downstream measures, then cluster them by maximizing their "modularity score" using established tools from network science. We find two surprising results: first, dropout dramatically increased modularity, while other forms of weight regularization had more modest effects. Second, although we observe that there is usually good agreement about clusters within both upstream methods and downstream methods, there is little agreement about the cluster assignments across these two families of methods. This has important implications for representation-learning, as it suggests that finding modular representations that reflect structure in inputs (e.g. disentanglement) may be a distinct goal from learning modular representations that reflect structure in outputs (e.g. compositionality).

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
papers.research_question: Does attention provide a faithful explanation for model decisions by identifying important input components?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not reliably interpretable as importance indicators; they are only noisy predictors of input components' importance to the model.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not an optimal method of identifying which attended elements are responsible for an output; as an importance ranking, it fails to explain model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
The highest attention weight often has a larger impact than a random weight, but there are many cases where the impact is similar.
Attention weights often fail to identify the minimal set of representations that are important for the model's decision.
Gradient-based rankings of attention weights often predict their effects better than their magnitudes.
The scope of contextualization (e.g., RNN vs. convolutional encoders) affects how well attention indicates importance.
In encoderless models, attention magnitudes are more helpful, but still not optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on text classification, which may not generalize to tasks with larger output spaces (e.g., language modeling).
Reliance on argmax decision flips as a measure of importance, which might be too coarse.
Only evaluated on specific attention functions (additive attention) and final layers; other variants and lower layers might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other tasks and models with larger output spaces.
Develop better, more informative importance rankings.
Align models with human feedback for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have recently boosted performance on a range of NLP tasks. Because attention layers explicitly weight input components' representations, it is also often assumed that attention can be used to identify information that models found important (e.g., specific contextualized word tokens). We test whether that assumption holds by manipulating attention weights in already-trained text classification models and analyzing the resulting differences in their predictions. While we observe some ways in which higher attention weights correlate with greater impact on model predictions, we also find many ways in which this does not hold, i.e., where gradient-based rankings of attention weights better predict their effects than their magnitudes. We conclude that while attention noisily predicts input components' overall importance to a model, it is by no means a fail-safe indicator. 1

papers.title: Clustering Head: A Visual Case Study of the Training Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn the sparse modular addition task, and what are the training dynamics and circuit structures that emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a visual sandbox to study training dynamics of transformers on the sparse modular addition task, revealing clustering head circuits that capture task invariants and analyzing two-phase learning and loss spikes.
papers.conclusion: The visual sandbox provides insights into transformer training dynamics and circuit formation, offering a foundation for understanding larger models and guiding practical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Introduces the sparse modular addition problem and a visual sandbox for visualizing transformer training dynamics.
Unveils clustering heads, circuits that learn the task's invariants (permutation and suffix invariance).
Observes a two-phase learning process: first clustering sequence embeddings, then fitting the MLP classifier.
Identifies loss spikes caused by high curvature in normalization layers and feedforward networks.
Shows that successful models tend to have denser activations and discusses the effects of initialization and curriculum learning.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on a small transformer with a synthetic task, which may not directly generalize to large-scale models and real-world tasks.
future_direction: Apply the visual sandbox to larger models and more complex tasks.
Investigate smoothing normalization layers to mitigate loss spikes.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the sparse modular addition task and examines how transformers learn it. We focus on transformers with embeddings in $\R^2$ and introduce a visual sandbox that provides comprehensive visualizations of each layer throughout the training process. We reveal a type of circuit, called "clustering heads," which learns the problem's invariants. We analyze the training dynamics of these circuits, highlighting two-stage learning, loss spikes due to high curvature or normalization layers, and the effects of initialization and curriculum learning.

papers.title: Easing Optimization Paths: a Circuit Perspective
papers.research_question: How does gradient descent interact with circuits in neural networks, and how can this perspective be used to design curricula for efficient learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using a circuit perspective to understand neural network training dynamics, demonstrating that gradient descent reinforces useful circuits and prunes others, and that curriculum learning can ease optimization by fostering sub-circuits.
papers.conclusion: The circuit perspective provides valuable insights into training dynamics and can be used to design curricula for efficient learning, with potential for advancing deep learning both practically and theoretically.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent reinforces useful circuits while pruning non-invariant ones during training.
Networks break down complex tasks into sub-circuits for intermediate reasoning steps.
Curriculum learning helps in discovering generalizing circuits by first learning simpler sub-tasks.
There is a loss barrier between memorizing and generalizing solutions, which curriculum learning helps overcome.
Visualization of attention dynamics shows how spurious circuits are pruned over time.
future_direction: Study the interplay between gradient norms, loss spikes, and training stability using a circuit perspective.
Study the impact of activation sparsity on models’ performance using a circuit perspective.
papers.abstract: Gradient descent is the method of choice for training large artificial intelligence systems. As these systems become larger, a better understanding of the mechanisms behind gradient training would allow us to alleviate compute costs and help steer these systems away from harmful behaviors. To that end, we suggest utilizing the circuit perspective brought forward by mechanistic interpretability. After laying out our intuition, we illustrate how it enables us to design a curriculum for efficient learning in a controlled setting. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/pal}.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs): Visual Explainability of Learned Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we discover and visualize learned concepts in neural network layers by analyzing activation patterns beyond individual neuron analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs), a method for layer-level concept discovery in neural networks by clustering activation profiles, providing a visual explainability tool.
papers.conclusion: NAPs provide a layer-level explainability method that complements existing techniques, enabling deeper understanding of neural network models through visual introspection of learned concepts.
papers.key_findings:
NAPs can reveal distinct concepts learned at different layers, such as low-level features in early layers and high-level concepts in later layers.
NAPs allow for comparison of concepts across different models, revealing architectural differences and performance variations.
NAPs can uncover biases in training data, such as overrepresentation of certain contexts (e.g., people holding fish).
The method is robust across various network architectures and datasets, from simple MNIST models to complex ImageNet models.
NAPs complement existing unit-level explainability methods by providing layer-level insights.
papers.limitation:
NAPs require human interpretation and may not always reflect what the model sees.
The discovery of NAPs depends on the input data used; if a concept is not present in the input data, it cannot be extracted.
Earlier layers tend to produce fewer and less interpretable NAPs because they represent low-level features.
future_direction: Applying NAPs to different data types and tasks, such as GANs, Transformers, and RNNs.
Combining NAPs with attribution methods to highlight input features representative of a NAP.
Slicing activations across different dimensions, such as classes, to find intra-class differences.
papers.abstract: A key to deciphering the inner workings of neural networks is understanding what a model has learned. Promising methods for discovering learned features are based on analyzing activation values, whereby current techniques focus on analyzing high activation values to reveal interesting features on a neuron level. However, analyzing high activation values limits layer-level concept discovery. We present a method that instead takes into account the entire activation distribution. By extracting similar activation profiles within the high-dimensional activation space of a neural network layer, we find groups of inputs that are treated similarly. These input groups represent neural activation patterns (NAPs) and can be used to visualize and interpret learned layer concepts. We release a framework with which NAPs can be extracted from pre-trained models and provide a visual introspection tool that can be used to analyze NAPs. We tested our method with a variety of networks and show how it complements existing methods for analyzing neural network activation values.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
Cholinergic modulation is a common mechanism that biases processing toward external modes across multiple systems.
future_direction: Test the prediction that disruption of mode-switching (e.g., between non-REM and REM sleep) impairs integration of new hippocampal memories with existing neocortical knowledge.
Investigate how altering the timescale of switching affects the learning of temporally extended features.
Explore the role of neuromodulators like acetylcholine in regulating mode-switching and learning across different brain systems.
papers.abstract: Brains construct internal models that support perception, prediction, and action in the external world. Individual circuits within a brain also learn internal models of the local world of input they receive, in order to facilitate efficient and robust representation. How are these internal models learned? We propose that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing. We review computational evidence that this mode-switching can produce an error signal to drive learning. We then consider empirical evidence for the instantiation of mode-switching in diverse neural systems, ranging from subsecond fluctuations in the hippocampus to wake-sleep alternations across the whole brain. We hypothesize that these internal/external switching processes, which occur at multiple scales, can drive learning at each scale. This framework predicts that (a) slower mode-switching should be associated with learning of more temporally extended input features and (b) disruption of switching should impair the integration of new information with prior information.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
