future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads in multi-head attention models, and can a large percentage be pruned at test time without significantly impacting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Many attention heads in trained multi-head attention models are redundant and can be pruned without significant performance loss, with encoder-decoder attention being more reliant on multiple heads than self-attention.
papers.conclusion: Multi-head attention does not always fully leverage its theoretical expressiveness, and pruning heads can improve inference efficiency without harming performance, offering insights for more parameter-efficient models.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention heads can be individually removed at test time without a statistically significant drop in performance.
Some entire attention layers can be reduced to a single head without impacting performance.
A greedy pruning algorithm based on a gradient-derived importance score can remove 20-40% of heads without noticeable performance degradation.
Encoder-decoder attention layers are much more sensitive to pruning than self-attention layers.
The distinction between important and unimportant heads increases as training progresses, suggesting training dynamics play a role.
future_direction: A more principled investigation of the training dynamics of head importance.
Inspiring models that invest their parameters and attention more efficiently.
papers.abstract: Attention is a powerful and ubiquitous mechanism for allowing neural models to focus on particular salient pieces of information by taking their weighted average when making predictions. In particular, multi-headed attention is a driving force behind many recent state-of-the-art NLP models such as Transformer-based MT models and BERT. These models apply multiple attention mechanisms in parallel, with each attention "head" potentially focusing on different parts of the input, which makes it possible to express sophisticated functions beyond the simple weighted average. In this paper we make the surprising observation that even if models have been trained using multiple heads, in practice, a large percentage of attention heads can be removed at test time without significantly impacting performance. In fact, some layers can even be reduced to a single head. We further examine greedy algorithms for pruning down models, and the potential speed, memory efficiency, and accuracy improvements obtainable therefrom. Finally, we analyze the results with respect to which parts of the model are more reliant on having multiple heads, and provide precursory evidence that training dynamics play a role in the gains provided by multi-head attention.

papers.title: Abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained to perform multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How do abstract (disentangled) representations emerge in neural networks? The paper investigates whether training on multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge.
papers.core_contribution: Training neural networks on multiple tasks causes abstract (disentangled) representations to emerge, which enables few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: Abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and could be pervasive in high-level brain regions.
papers.key_findings:
Abstract representations emerge when the number of tasks (P) exceeds the number of latent variables (D).
These representations are robust to task heterogeneity, including unbalanced tasks, contextual tasks, and partial information.
Abstract representations emerge with both supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
The multi-tasking model produces abstract representations from image inputs (2D shapes and 3D chairs).
Abstract representations enable few-sample learning and generalization to novel tasks.
future_direction: Test the predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly in neural data.
Investigate abstract representations in more complex neural network architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract Humans and other animals demonstrate a remarkable ability to generalize knowledge across distinct contexts and objects during natural behavior. We posit that this ability to generalize arises from a specific representational geometry, that we call abstract and that is referred to as disentangled in machine learning. These abstract representations have been observed in recent neurophysiological studies. However, it is unknown how they emerge. Here, using feedforward neural networks, we demonstrate that the learning of multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge, using both supervised and reinforcement learning. We show that these abstract representations enable few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks. We conclude that abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and, as a consequence, could be pervasive in high-level brain regions. We also make several specific predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly.

papers.title: Peer Review #3 of "Learning to perform role-filler binding with schematic knowledge (v0.2)"
papers.core_contribution: Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) can learn to perform role-filler binding without explicit labels and generalize to arbitrary fillers, even those that violate training correlations, by storing bindings in their external memory components.
papers.conclusion: Networks with external memory can learn role-filler binding, a key component for learning flexible, structured cognitive representations, by extracting relations from input structure rather than relying on training correlations.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) learn to perform role-filler binding without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs.
These networks can generalize to previously unseen fillers when trained with an unlimited pool of fillers (Unlimited Filler Training).
The Fast Weights network shows biases towards statistical regularities from training, while the DNC does not, suggesting different binding mechanisms.
Decoding analyses indicate successful networks store role-filler bindings in their external memory components (fast weights matrix or memory buffer), not in the controller's hidden state.
Networks fail when test stories are presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training, indicating reliance on structural similarities.
papers.limitation:
Networks fail when given stories presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training.
The study does not prove that all standard RNN and LSTM models are unable to solve these tasks; future work with larger LSTMs might succeed.
future_direction: Training regimes that use shuffled stories during training to make models robust to test stories with shuffled segments.
Investigating how much a pool of train fillers needs to be expanded to allow networks to learn a representation that extends to previously unseen fillers.
Testing models of role-filler binding against neural data, potentially using paradigms for probing activity-silent memory.
papers.abstract: Through specific experiences, humans learn the relationships that underlie the structure of events in the world. Schema theory suggests that we organize this information in mental frameworks called "schemata," which represent our knowledge of the structure of the world. Generalizing knowledge of structural relationships to new situations requires rolefiller binding, the ability to associate specific "fillers" with abstract "roles." For instance, when we hear the sentence "Alice ordered a tea from Bob," the role-filler bindings "Alice:customer," "tea:drink," and "Bob:barista" allow us to understand and make inferences about the sentence. We can perform these bindings for arbitrary fillers -we understand this sentence even if we have never heard the names "Alice," "tea," or "Bob" before. In this work, we define a model as capable of performing role-filler binding if it can recall arbitrary fillers corresponding to a specified role, even when these pairings violate correlations seen during training. Previous work found that models can learn this ability when explicitly told what the roles and fillers are, or when given fillers seen during training. We show that networks with external memory learn to bind roles to arbitrary fillers, without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs. We further show that they can perform these bindings on role-filler pairs that violate correlations seen during training, while retaining knowledge of training correlations. We apply analyses inspired by neural decoding to interpret what the networks have learned.

papers.title: Counterfactual Divergence Singularity: A Theoretical Model of High-Similarity Instability and Micro-Counterfactual Drift in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the relationship between input similarity and output divergence in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations be formalized, and what explains the instability near high similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS), a theoretical framework that characterizes instability in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations, showing that divergence increases sharply as semantic similarity approaches unity.
papers.conclusion: The Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS) captures instability in LLMs under micro-counterfactual perturbations, reframing challenges like hallucination as manifestations of local non-smoothness in semantic manifolds, and suggests new evaluation paradigms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Divergence exhibits a hyperbolic blow-up as semantic similarity approaches 1.
Semantic curvature increases logarithmically in high-similarity regimes.
Embedding drift is minimal for high-similarity pairs, but divergence is high, indicating a contradiction.
LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth, leading to instability near the identity boundary.
The CDS phenomenon provides a geometric explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Scale and computational constraints with only 200 micro-counterfactual pairs.
Dependency on a single paraphraser (FLAN-T5-Base).
Dependence on a single embedding model (SBERT MiniLM-L6-v2).
Absence of output-level probability divergence analysis.
Limited to English-language textual inputs.
Interpretational boundaries, not claiming CDS explains all hallucinations.
future_direction: Scaling to larger datasets (e.g., 2,000–20,000 pairs).
Testing with different paraphrasers and embedding models.
Including output-level probability divergence analysis.
Extending to other languages and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable fluency and contextual sensitivity, yet their behaviour under minimal semantic perturbations remains poorly understood. In particular, near-identical paraphrastic inputs—expected to yield stable and equivalent responses—often produce disproportionately divergent generative behaviour. This paper introduces the <bold>Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS)</bold> , a theoretical and empirical framework that characterizes a previously underexplored instability regime in transformer-based language models. This work formalizes micro-counterfactual perturbations as infinitesimal semantic variations in embedding space and show that, as semantic similarity approaches unity, divergence metrics exhibit a hyperbolic blow-up. Using a controlled experimental pipeline based on FLAN-T5-generated paraphrases and Sentence-BERT semantic embeddings, this paper empirically demonstrate that divergence, curvature, and embedding drift collectively reveal a singular boundary where semantic proximity no longer guarantees behavioural stability. Despite minimal embedding displacement and near-maximal cosine similarity, reciprocal divergence measures increase sharply, exposing a structural nonlinearity in the input–output mapping of LLMs. The results suggest that LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth and that standard embedding-based similarity metrics fail to capture instability near the identity boundary. This phenomenon provides a geometric and mathematical explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and certain forms of hallucination observed in generative systems. By reframing these behaviours as consequences of latent-space singularities rather than isolated decoding artifacts, this work contributes a novel theoretical lens for evaluating robustness, interpretability, and reliability in large language models.

papers.title: Word Order Matters When You Increase Masking
papers.research_question: To what extent do masked language models require explicit position encoding to perform well on the masked language modeling objective, and how does the amount of masking affect this requirement?
papers.core_contribution: The utility of explicit position encoding in masked language models increases with the number of masked tokens; without position encoding, models cannot reconstruct position information when masking is high.
papers.conclusion: Position encoding becomes necessary for masked language modeling as the amount of masking increases, and the amount of masking should be carefully chosen to encourage models to use position information.
papers.key_findings:
When only one token is masked, models with and without position encoding perform similarly.
As the number of masked tokens increases, the true probability distribution for ordered contexts diverges from that of unordered contexts.
Models with position encoding (BERT) approximate the ordered distribution well, while models without (NP) approximate the unordered distribution.
The amount of masking is a crucial parameter for models to use position information.
papers.limitation:
The results are obtained on artificial languages, and adapting the method to natural languages may be difficult because the true probability distribution is not accessible.
Training multiple models on natural languages is computationally expensive.
The artificial language has fixed word order, so the findings may not generalize to natural languages with more flexible word order.
future_direction: Find proxies to estimate reference points for natural languages.
Evaluate impact of position encoding in languages with variable word order.
papers.abstract: Word order, an essential property of natural languages, is injected in Transformer-based neural language models using position encoding. However, recent experiments have shown that explicit position encoding is not always useful, since some models without such feature managed to achieve state-of-the art performance on some tasks. To understand better this phenomenon, we examine the effect of removing position encodings on the pre-training objective itself (i.e., masked language modelling), to test whether models can reconstruct position information from co-occurrences alone. We do so by controlling the amount of masked tokens in the input sentence, as a proxy to affect the importance of position information for the task. We find that the necessity of position information increases with the amount of masking, and that masked language models without position encodings are not able to reconstruct this information on the task. These findings point towards a direct relationship between the amount of masking and the ability of Transformers to capture order-sensitive aspects of language using position encoding.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Emergent Low-Rank Training Dynamics in MLPs with Smooth Activations
papers.research_question: How do training dynamics in MLPs with smooth activations concentrate within low-dimensional subspaces, and can this be leveraged for low-rank parameterization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that weight dynamics in MLPs with smooth activations concentrate in low-dimensional subspaces, theoretically characterizes these subspaces for two-layer networks, and proposes a low-rank MLP parameterization that matches full-rank performance with proper initialization.
papers.conclusion: Training dynamics of MLPs with smooth activations are low-dimensional, enabling effective low-rank parameterizations that match full-rank performance with proper initialization.
papers.key_findings:
For MLPs with smooth activations, weight updates are concentrated in low-dimensional subspaces that depend on initialization.
Theoretically, for two-layer networks, gradient updates are mostly in a rank-2K subspace.
Empirically, the phenomenon extends to deeper networks, different optimizers, and unwhitened data.
A low-rank MLP parameterization with proper initialization can match full-rank performance on classification tasks.
Initialization of the low-rank factors is crucial; random initialization leads to poor performance.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis assumes whitened input data, fixed second layer, and small initialization scale.
Theoretical results are limited to two-layer networks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other architectures and activation functions
Design efficient low-rank training algorithms
papers.abstract: Recent empirical evidence has demonstrated that the training dynamics of large-scale deep neural networks occur within low-dimensional subspaces. While this has inspired new research into low-rank training, compression, and adaptation, theoretical justification for these dynamics in nonlinear networks remains limited. %compared to deep linear settings. To address this gap, this paper analyzes the learning dynamics of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) under gradient descent (GD). We demonstrate that the weight dynamics concentrate within invariant low-dimensional subspaces throughout training. Theoretically, we precisely characterize these invariant subspaces for two-layer networks with smooth nonlinear activations, providing insight into their emergence. Experimentally, we validate that this phenomenon extends beyond our theoretical assumptions. Leveraging these insights, we empirically show there exists a low-rank MLP parameterization that, when initialized within the appropriate subspaces, matches the classification performance of fully-parameterized counterparts on a variety of classification tasks.

papers.title: Identifying Equivalent Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we identify equivalent training dynamics in deep neural networks? The paper proposes using topological conjugacy and Koopman operator theory to address this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Koopman operator theory-based framework to identify topologically conjugate training dynamics in deep neural networks, enabling the comparison of training dynamics across architectures and hyperparameters.
papers.conclusion: The Koopman-based framework is flexible and can shed new light on training dynamics across a range of DNN architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The framework correctly identifies the known topological conjugacy between online mirror descent and online gradient descent.
Narrow and wide fully connected neural networks exhibit non-conjugate training dynamics.
Different random initializations of wide FCNs can lead to conjugate training dynamics.
Convolutional neural networks show early training dynamics transitions, but LeNet and ResNet-20 have non-conjugate dynamics.
Transformers that undergo grokking and those that do not have non-conjugate training dynamics.
papers.limitation:
Numerical approximations of Koopman mode decomposition are only approximations and are subject to hyperparameter selection, choice of observable functions, and number of modes considered.
Assessing whether Koopman eigenvalues are sufficiently similar to indicate conjugacy is challenging; the Wasserstein distance and randomized shuffle control have limitations.
future_direction: Data-driven discovery and generation of new classes of optimization algorithms.
Learning mappings that transform one DNN model to another.
Characterizing Koopman eigenvalues across a wide range of DNN models to improve training methods.
papers.abstract: Study of the nonlinear evolution deep neural network (DNN) parameters undergo during training has uncovered regimes of distinct dynamical behavior. While a detailed understanding of these phenomena has the potential to advance improvements in training efficiency and robustness, the lack of methods for identifying when DNN models have equivalent dynamics limits the insight that can be gained from prior work. Topological conjugacy, a notion from dynamical systems theory, provides a precise definition of dynamical equivalence, offering a possible route to address this need. However, topological conjugacies have historically been challenging to compute. By leveraging advances in Koopman operator theory, we develop a framework for identifying conjugate and non-conjugate training dynamics. To validate our approach, we demonstrate that comparing Koopman eigenvalues can correctly identify a known equivalence between online mirror descent and online gradient descent. We then utilize our approach to: (a) identify non-conjugate training dynamics between shallow and wide fully connected neural networks; (b) characterize the early phase of training dynamics in convolutional neural networks; (c) uncover non-conjugate training dynamics in Transformers that do and do not undergo grokking. Our results, across a range of DNN architectures, illustrate the flexibility of our framework and highlight its potential for shedding new light on training dynamics.

papers.title: On the Cone Effect in the Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) evolve during neural network training, and what are the characteristics of the learning dynamics in real-world settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'cone effect' in the late-phase learning dynamics of neural networks, where the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) continues to evolve but within a constrained function space, providing significant performance advantages over the fully linearized (lazy) training regime.
papers.conclusion: The work unveils a cone effect in the late learning dynamics of neural networks, where the eNTK evolves in a constrained space during Phase II, offering performance advantages over the lazy regime, though this phenomenon is not universal.
papers.key_findings:
The learning dynamics exhibit a two-phase process: Phase I with significant eNTK evolution (rich regime) and Phase II where the eNTK evolves within a constrained space (cone effect).
The cone effect in Phase II provides non-negligible performance benefits over training solely in the lazy regime, as shown by a switching experiment from standard to linearized training.
The two-phase hypothesis and cone effect are not universal, as a counterexample (LeNet on MNIST) shows continuous kernel evolution without a clear two-phase pattern.
papers.limitation: The cone effect and two-phase hypothesis are not universal, as demonstrated by a counterexample (LeNet on MNIST) where the kernel keeps evolving without a clear two-phase pattern.
future_direction: Further efforts on uncovering the contributing factors of the cone effect are expected.
papers.abstract: Understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks is a central topic in the deep learning community. In this paper, we take an empirical perspective to study the learning dynamics of neural networks in real-world settings. Specifically, we investigate the evolution process of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) during training. Our key findings reveal a two-phase learning process: i) in Phase I, the eNTK evolves significantly, signaling the rich regime, and ii) in Phase II, the eNTK keeps evolving but is constrained in a narrow space, a phenomenon we term the cone effect. This two-phase framework builds on the hypothesis proposed by Fort et al. (2020), but we uniquely identify the cone effect in Phase II, demonstrating its significant performance advantages over fully linearized training.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: On the geometry of generalization and memorization in deep neural\n networks
papers.research_question: How does memorization of training data occur across the layers of a deep neural network, and what is the connection between the geometry of internal representations and generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization in deep neural networks occurs predominantly in the deeper layers due to decreasing manifold radius and dimension, while early layers learn general features; generalization can be restored by rewinding the final few layers' weights to an earlier epoch.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals the layer-wise structure of memorization in deep networks, showing it is concentrated in deeper layers and driven by geometric properties of representations, and links the double descent phenomenon to manifold geometry.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization occurs abruptly in the deeper layers of the network, while early layers learn general features that are minimally affected by label noise.
The geometry of object manifolds (capacity, radius, dimension) changes with depth and training time, and these geometric properties are linked to memorization and generalization.
Generalization performance can be largely restored by rewinding the parameters of the final few layers to an earlier epoch before significant memorization occurred.
The double descent phenomenon in generalization with increasing model size is linked to a non-monotonic change in the dimensionality of the object manifolds.
Gradient analysis shows that early in training, the gradient contribution from permuted (noise) examples is small, causing the network to initially ignore noise and learn shared features.
papers.abstract:
Understanding how large neural networks avoid memorizing training data is key
to explaining their high generalization performance. To examine the structure
of when and where memorization occurs in a deep network, we use a recently
developed replica-based mean field theoretic geometric analysis method. We find
that all layers preferentially learn from examples which share features, and
link this behavior to generalization performance. Memorization predominately
occurs in the deeper layers, due to decreasing object manifolds' radius and
dimension, whereas early layers are minimally affected. This predicts that
generalization can be restored by reverting the final few layer weights to
earlier epochs before significant memorization occurred, which is confirmed by
the experiments. Additionally, by studying generalization under different model
sizes, we reveal the connection between the double descent phenomenon and the
underlying model geometry. Finally, analytical analysis shows that networks
avoid memorization early in training because close to initialization, the
gradient contribution from permuted examples are small. These findings provide
quantitative evidence for the structure of memorization across layers of a deep
neural network, the drivers for such structure, and its connection to manifold
geometric properties.

papers.title: Contribution of task-irrelevant stimuli to drift of neural representations
papers.research_question: How do task-irrelevant stimuli contribute to representational drift in neural networks during online learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that task-irrelevant stimuli act as a source of noise in online learning, causing representational drift in neural networks across various architectures and learning rules.
papers.conclusion: The study links the structure of stimuli, task, and learning rule to representational drift, providing a theoretical foundation for using drift as a signal to uncover underlying computation in neural systems.
papers.key_findings:
Drift rate increases with the variance and dimension of task-irrelevant stimuli.
This phenomenon holds for Hebbian-based learning (Oja's rule, Similarity Matching) and stochastic gradient descent (autoencoder, two-layer network).
Drift due to learning noise has different geometric and dimension-dependency predictions than drift caused by Gaussian synaptic noise.
In MNIST data, drift rate peaks at an intermediate bottleneck dimension due to trade-off between representational space and noise from task-irrelevant stimuli.
Nonlinear networks with localized receptive fields also exhibit increased drift with task-irrelevant variance.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical derivations are limited to linear networks.
The framework assumes small learning rates and fluctuations around the solution.
The study does not consider task-irrelevant stimuli appearing in separate contexts.
future_direction: Future experiments controlling the amount of task-irrelevant stimuli to test predictions.
Extending the theory to nonlinear networks and large learning rates.
Investigating drift in contexts where task-irrelevant stimuli appear separately.
papers.abstract: Biological and artificial learners are inherently exposed to a stream of data and experience throughout their lifetimes and must constantly adapt to, learn from, or selectively ignore the ongoing input. Recent findings reveal that, even when the performance remains stable, the underlying neural representations can change gradually over time, a phenomenon known as representational drift. Studying the different sources of data and noise that may contribute to drift is essential for understanding lifelong learning in neural systems. However, a systematic study of drift across architectures and learning rules, and the connection to task, are missing. Here, in an online learning setup, we characterize drift as a function of data distribution, and specifically show that the learning noise induced by task-irrelevant stimuli, which the agent learns to ignore in a given context, can create long-term drift in the representation of task-relevant stimuli. Using theory and simulations, we demonstrate this phenomenon both in Hebbian-based learning -- Oja's rule and Similarity Matching -- and in stochastic gradient descent applied to autoencoders and a supervised two-layer network. We consistently observe that the drift rate increases with the variance and the dimension of the data in the task-irrelevant subspace. We further show that this yields different qualitative predictions for the geometry and dimension-dependency of drift than those arising from Gaussian synaptic noise. Overall, our study links the structure of stimuli, task, and learning rule to representational drift and could pave the way for using drift as a signal for uncovering underlying computation in the brain.

papers.title: Hypernym Bias: Unraveling Deep Classifier Training Dynamics through the Lens of Class Hierarchy
papers.research_question: What patterns do neural networks learn first and last? Specifically, how do hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Networks learn hypernyms (higher-level categories) earlier than hyponyms (specific categories) during training, and we introduce a framework to track this hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Hypernym bias is a consistent phenomenon across architectures and datasets, providing a framework for studying training dynamics and connecting early training bias to neural collapse.
papers.key_findings:
Hypernyms reach near maximum recognition accuracy early in training.
The learned representations align with the semantic structure of the dataset (WordNet).
Neural collapse properties appear earlier in hypernym label spaces.
The phenomenon is consistent across architectures (ResNet, ViT, MobileNet) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, DBPedia).
The training dynamics can be interpreted as top-to-bottom hierarchical label clustering.
papers.limitation:
The hierarchical structure of WordNet is imperfect and may not fully capture class relationships.
The phenomenon is less pronounced in datasets with less defined hierarchies (e.g., CIFAR-100).
future_direction: Extend the notion of hypernym bias to other domains (e.g., AudioSet).
Learn class hierarchies through data-driven hierarchical clustering instead of relying on external structures.
Investigate theoretical connections between hypernym bias and other known biases (e.g., simplicity bias, frequency principle).
papers.abstract: We investigate the training dynamics of deep classifiers by examining how hierarchical relationships between classes evolve during training. Through extensive experiments, we argue that the learning process in classification problems can be understood through the lens of label clustering. Specifically, we observe that networks tend to distinguish higher-level (hypernym) categories in the early stages of training, and learn more specific (hyponym) categories later. We introduce a novel framework to track the evolution of the feature manifold during training, revealing how the hierarchy of class relations emerges and refines across the network layers. Our analysis demonstrates that the learned representations closely align with the semantic structure of the dataset, providing a quantitative description of the clustering process. Notably, we show that in the hypernym label space, certain properties of neural collapse appear earlier than in the hyponym label space, helping to bridge the gap between the initial and terminal phases of learning. We believe our findings offer new insights into the mechanisms driving hierarchical learning in deep networks, paving the way for future advancements in understanding deep learning dynamics.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of BERT Token Representations to Explain Sentence Probing Results
papers.research_question: What role do specific token representations play in BERT's ability to encode linguistic features and explain probing results?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes linguistic features in specific token representations, and gradient-based attribution can reveal these subspaces to explain probing performance.
papers.conclusion: BERT's token representations encode specific linguistic knowledge, and attribution methods provide insights into probing results, revealing distinct subspaces for different features.
papers.key_findings:
Sentence-ending tokens retain positional information in higher layers.
The ##s token encodes both noun number and verb tense information, and BERT separates these usages into distinct subspaces.
In bi-gram shift tasks, inverted tokens have higher attribution scores, and abnormalities are encoded in their representations.
In coordination inversion, coordinators like 'and' and 'but' play a key role, and their representations change significantly.
Attribution patterns are consistent even with less training data, indicating that knowledge is well-encoded in representations.
future_direction: Investigate how subspaces evolve during fine-tuning
Check if behaviors are affected by different training objectives
Use token-level analysis for model efficiency
papers.abstract: Several studies have been carried out on revealing linguistic features captured by BERT. This is usually achieved by training a diagnostic classifier on the representations obtained from different layers of BERT. The subsequent classification accuracy is then interpreted as the ability of the model in encoding the corresponding linguistic property. Despite providing insights, these studies have left out the potential role of token representations. In this paper, we provide a more in-depth analysis on the representation space of BERT in search for distinct and meaningful subspaces that can explain the reasons behind these probing results. Based on a set of probing tasks and with the help of attribution methods we show that BERT tends to encode meaningful knowledge in specific token representations (which are often ignored in standard classification setups), allowing the model to detect syntactic and semantic abnormalities, and to distinctively separate grammatical number and tense subspaces. 1

papers.title: Studying the Evolution of Neural Activation Patterns During Training of Feed-Forward ReLU Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural activation patterns evolve during training for different network architectures and training strategies? Specifically, the paper investigates the retention of initialization information, the order and timing of structural convergence, the evolution of functional expressivity, and the confirmation of known early-training dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a technique to efficiently record activation statistics (e.g., entropy, pattern similarity) during training and uses it to analyze the evolution of activation patterns in ReLU networks, revealing architecture- and method-specific behavioral patterns.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of activation patterns provides new insights into the discrete optimization process during neural network training, connecting architectural and training method choices to the resulting changes in network structure and expressivity.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns change most rapidly in the early phase of training, with many patterns from initialization being replaced quickly.
Residual networks (ResNets) retain a higher proportion of activation patterns from initialization compared to networks without skip connections.
Activation entropy (a measure of expressivity) typically drops after the first few training steps and then recovers, with architecture-specific curves; ResNets maintain higher expressivity.
PyramidNet and ResNet with FixUp initialization show more uniform convergence of activation patterns across layers, in contrast to the bottom-up convergence seen in conventional CNNs.
The distribution of activation patterns confirms known observations about the early phase of training, such as rapid changes and the impact of unfavorable batches.
papers.abstract: The ability of deep neural networks to form powerful emergent representations of complex statistical patterns in data is as remarkable as imperfectly understood. For deep ReLU networks, these are encoded in the mixed discrete-continuous structure of linear weight matrices and non-linear binary activations. Our article develops a new technique for instrumenting such networks to efficiently record activation statistics, such as information content (entropy) and similarity of patterns, in real-world training runs. We then study the evolution of activation patterns during training for networks of different architecture using different training and initialization strategies. As a result, we see characteristic- and general-related as well as architecture-related behavioral patterns: in particular, most architectures form bottom-up structure, with the exception of highly tuned state-of-the-art architectures and methods (PyramidNet and FixUp), where layers appear to converge more simultaneously. We also observe intermediate dips in entropy in conventional CNNs that are not visible in residual networks. A reference implementation is provided under a free license.

papers.title: Interpreting Recurrent and Attention-Based Neural Models: a Case Study on Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the intermediate layers (attention and LSTM gating signals) of neural models for Natural Language Inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces saliency-based visualization methods for interpreting attention and LSTM gating signals in neural models for Natural Language Inference, revealing insights into model decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization and interpretation strategies for neural models provide insights into how and why they work, demonstrating effectiveness on the complex NLI task.
papers.key_findings:
Attention saliency maps highlight which word alignments critically contribute to the model's prediction, whereas standard attention visualizations do not.
Comparing models via attention saliency reveals differences in focus; ESIM-300 correctly attends to gender connections while ESIM-50 does not.
Saliency patterns of LSTM gating signals differ across examples and can identify sentence parts important for the model's decision.
The inference LSTM shows more concentrated saliency on key sentence parts compared to the more spread-out saliency in the input LSTM.
Forward and backward LSTMs provide complementary understanding, sometimes focusing on different parts of the sentence.
future_direction: Extend the study to other NLP tasks and models to produce useful insights for further improving these models.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in natural language inference (NLI) tasks. While these models are widely explored, they are hard to interpret and it is often unclear how and why they actually work. In this paper, we take a step toward explaining such deep learning based models through a case study on a popular neural model for NLI.

papers.title: Detecting Learning vs Memorization in Deep Neural Networks using Shared Structure Validation Sets
papers.research_question: How can we differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained with real labels, as opposed to shuffled labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel permutation approach using shared structure validation sets (s-validation sets) and shallow classifiers to differentiate between learning and memorization in DNNs trained with real labels.
papers.conclusion: The proposed permutation approach using s-validation sets provides a useful tool for understanding how DNNs memorize and learn over training epochs.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs can simultaneously learn and memorize during training.
Regularization (e.g., dropout) and increasing the number of layers can reduce memorization.
DNNs exhibit dynamic memorization patterns over training epochs, with an initial memorization phase followed by a forgetting phase.
Surprisingly, DNNs can learn from pure Gaussian noise inputs, not just memorize them.
The method is useful for relative comparisons of memorization between different DNNs, but not for absolute quantification.
papers.limitation: The method cannot quantify the absolute amount of memorization in a DNN, only relative comparisons between models.
papers.abstract: The roles played by learning and memorization represent an important topic in deep learning research. Recent work on this subject has shown that the optimization behavior of DNNs trained on shuffled labels is qualitatively different from DNNs trained with real labels. Here, we propose a novel permutation approach that can differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained as usual (i.e., using the real labels to guide the learning, rather than shuffled labels). The evaluation of weather the DNN has learned and/or memorized, happens in a separate step where we compare the predictive performance of a shallow classifier trained with the features learned by the DNN, against multiple instances of the same classifier, trained on the same input, but using shuffled labels as outputs. By evaluating these shallow classifiers in validation sets that share structure with the training set, we are able to tell apart learning from memorization. Application of our permutation approach to multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks trained on image data corroborated many findings from other groups. Most importantly, our illustrations also uncovered interesting dynamic patterns about how DNNs memorize over increasing numbers of training epochs, and support the surprising result that DNNs are still able to learn, rather than only memorize, when trained with pure Gaussian noise as input.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Predicate learning in neural systems: Discovering latent generative structures
papers.research_question: How can latent representational structures (predicates) be learned from experience with unstructured data in neural systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains how predicate learning enables neural systems to discover latent generative structures from unstructured data using intersective comparison and neural oscillations, supporting compositionality and human-like generalization.
papers.conclusion: Predicate learning demonstrates how symbolic structures can be learned from neural signals, linking computational principles to neurophysiology and enabling complex human-like behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Predicate learning uses intersective comparison to detect invariants and form latent structures from unstructured data.
Neural oscillations, specifically desynchronization, enable dynamic binding of predicates and arguments without altering their meanings.
This approach allows for compositionality through rhythmic computation, facilitating the generation of new representations.
Predicate learning supports extrapolatory generalization to unseen data, as demonstrated in video game tasks.
It bridges symbolic representations and neural computation, offering insights into human cognitive processes.
papers.abstract: Humans learn complex latent structures from their environments (e.g., natural language, mathematics, music, social hierarchies). In cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience, models that infer higher-order structures from sensory or first-order representations have been proposed to account for the complexity and flexibility of human behavior. But how do the structures that these models invoke arise in neural systems in the first place? To answer this question, we explain how a system can learn latent representational structures (i.e., predicates) from experience with wholly unstructured data. During the process of predicate learning, an artificial neural network exploits the naturally occurring dynamic properties of distributed computing across neuronal assemblies in order to learn predicates, but also to combine them compositionally, two computational aspects which appear to be necessary for human behavior as per formal theories in multiple domains. We describe how predicates can be combined generatively using neural oscillations to achieve human-like extrapolation and compositionality in an artificial neural network. The ability to learn predicates from experience, to represent structures compositionally, and to extrapolate to unseen data offers an inroads to understanding and modeling the most complex human behaviors.

papers.title: Meta-Learning Neural Mechanisms rather than Bayesian Priors
papers.research_question: What does meta-learning imbue models with? Does it learn simplicity-based priors or neural mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (e.g., counters) into models, rather than learning simplicity-based priors, providing efficient meta-learning paradigms and theoretical insights linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Meta-trained models do not mimic the statistical properties of their meta-training dataset; instead, they acquire useful neural mechanisms, and meta-training on mechanistically-complex languages is vital for encouraging such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Models meta-trained on simplicity-bias datasets do not outperform those on complexity-bias datasets, contradicting the simplicity-bias view.
Meta-training on a single formal language can be as effective as meta-training on 5000 different languages if the language incentivizes useful neural mechanisms.
Meta-training on context-free and context-sensitive languages outperforms meta-training on regular languages, indicating mechanistic complexity matters.
GRUs do not show the same meta-learning improvement as LSTMs, likely because they cannot acquire counting mechanisms.
The Chomsky hierarchy may not fully capture the neural mechanisms useful for a given architecture, suggesting need for alternative hierarchies.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to formal language learning and does not look at more complicated domains like natural language.
The work does not explicitly examine hidden layers to find the presence of neural counters.
future_direction: Investigate alternative theoretical hierarchies that correspond to neural mechanisms useful in specific architectures.
Explore meta-learning in different architectures beyond LSTMs and GRUs, such as Transformers or Stack-RNNs.
Develop computational hierarchies akin to the Chomsky hierarchy but defined in terms of neural architectures and their mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Children acquire language despite being exposed to several orders of magnitude less data than large language models require. Meta-learning has been proposed as a way to integrate human-like learning biases into neural-network architectures, combining both the structured generalizations of symbolic models with the scalability of neural-network models. But what does meta-learning exactly imbue the model with? We investigate the meta-learning of formal languages and find that, contrary to previous claims, meta-trained models are not learning simplicity-based priors when meta-trained on datasets organised around simplicity. Rather, we find evidence that meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (such as counters) into the model, which function like cognitive primitives for the network on downstream tasks. Most surprisingly, we find that meta-training on a single formal language can provide as much improvement to a model as meta-training on 5000 different formal languages, provided that the formal language incentivizes the learning of useful neural mechanisms. Taken together, our findings provide practical implications for efficient meta-learning paradigms and new theoretical insights into linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.

papers.title: The Underlying Correlated Dynamics in Neural Training
papers.research_question: Can the dynamics of neural network parameters during training be modeled by grouping parameters into highly correlated modes, and does this representation reduce dimensionality and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Correlation Mode Decomposition (CMD), a method to model neural network training dynamics by clustering parameters into highly correlated groups (modes), which dramatically reduces dimensionality and can induce regularization for better generalization.
papers.conclusion: CMD is an effective method for modeling neural network training dynamics, reducing dimensionality, and improving generalization, paving the way for better network analysis and acceleration techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters during training can be grouped into a few highly correlated modes, providing a low-dimensional representation of the dynamics.
CMD induces regularization, leading to more stable training and improved test performance compared to original gradient descent.
CMD is robust to the number of modes and the sampling of weights for clustering.
CMD outperforms Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) in modeling training dynamics, especially with augmentations and complex architectures.
The typical time profiles of modes are spread throughout the network across all layers.
papers.limitation: CMD is applied post-training and requires checkpointing at each epoch, which can be memory-consuming for large models.
future_direction: Using CMD for network analysis and designing acceleration techniques.
papers.abstract: Training of neural networks is a computationally intensive task. The significance of understanding and modeling the training dynamics is growing as increasingly larger networks are being trained. We propose in this work a model based on the correlation of the parameters' dynamics, which dramatically reduces the dimensionality. We refer to our algorithm as \emph{correlation mode decomposition} (CMD). It splits the parameter space into groups of parameters (modes) which behave in a highly correlated manner through the epochs. We achieve a remarkable dimensionality reduction with this approach, where networks like ResNet-18, transformers and GANs, containing millions of parameters, can be modeled well using just a few modes. We observe each typical time profile of a mode is spread throughout the network in all layers. Moreover, our model induces regularization which yields better generalization capacity on the test set. This representation enhances the understanding of the underlying training dynamics and can pave the way for designing better acceleration techniques.

papers.title: Better Pre-Training by Reducing Representation Confusion
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to reduce two types of information confusion in pre-trained language models: confusion between distance and direction in relative position encoding, and high similarity between token representations and between head representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two techniques to reduce information confusion in pre-training: DDRP encoding decouples distance and direction in relative position encoding, and MTH objective reduces similarity between token and head representations, leading to improved performance and faster pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reducing information confusion in representation learning through DDRP and MTH improves pre-trained language models, and suggests broader applications of this principle.
papers.key_findings:
DDRP outperforms classical relative position encoding (BERT-R) and other baselines (TUPE, DEBERTA) on GLUE tasks without additional computational overhead.
MTH outperforms MLM by 0.96 average GLUE score and achieves nearly 2x pre-training speedup on BERTBASE.
DDRP reduces the number of parameters for relative position encoding from 2*rs to rs+3.
MTH reduces the average cosine self-similarity of token and head representations, leading to more discriminative representations.
DDRP exhibits a stronger directional bias in attention heads, with 92.11% of sentences showing an up-down triangle effect compared to 78.94% for BERT-R.
papers.limitation: The proposed methods induce additional computational costs: DDRP increases computational cost by about 5% compared to BERT, and MTH increases cost by about 4% compared to MLM.
future_direction: Exploring broader application scenarios for reducing information confusion in representation learning.
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the Transformer-based pre-trained language models and identify two different types of information confusion in position encoding and model representations, respectively. Firstly, we show that in the relative position encoding, the joint modeling about relative distances and directions brings confusion between two heterogeneous information. It may make the model unable to capture the associative semantics of the same distance and the opposite directions, which in turn affects the performance of downstream tasks. Secondly, we notice the BERT with Mask Language Modeling (MLM) pre-training objective outputs similar token representations (last hidden states of different tokens) and head representations (attention weightsof different heads), which may make the diversity of information expressed by different tokens and heads limited.Motivated by the above investigation, we propose two novel techniques to improve pre-trained language models: Decoupled Directional Relative Position (DDRP) encoding and MTH pre-training objective. DDRP decouples the relative distance features and the directional features in classical relative position encoding. MTH applies two novel auxiliary regularizers besides MLM to enlarge the dissimilarities between (a) last hidden states of different tokens, and (b) attention weights of different heads. These designs allow the model to capture different categories of information more clearly, as a way to alleviate information confusion in representation learning for better optimization.Extensive experiments and ablation studies on GLUE benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Lazy vs hasty: linearization in deep networks impacts learning schedule based on example difficulty
