papers.research_question: What is the comparative effect of the lazy (linear) and feature learning (non-linear) regimes on the training dynamics of various groups of examples of increasing difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: In the feature learning (non-linear) regime, easy examples are given more weight and learned faster compared to difficult ones, leading to a sequential learning schedule based on example difficulty.
papers.conclusion: The non-linear (feature learning) regime prioritizes easy examples, resulting in a sequential learning schedule that can be beneficial for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Easy examples are learned faster in the non-linear regime compared to the linear regime.
The non-linear regime shows a more pronounced simplicity bias, prioritizing easy examples.
In the presence of label noise, the non-linear regime delays memorization of noisy examples, leading to better generalization.
In spurious correlation setups, the non-linear regime is more prone to learning the spurious feature initially.
Theoretical analysis in a quadratic model confirms that non-linearity induces sequential learning of modes based on their difficulty.
papers.abstract: Among attempts at giving a theoretical account of the success of deep neural networks, a recent line of work has identified a so-called lazy training regime in which the network can be well approximated by its linearization around initialization. Here we investigate the comparative effect of the lazy (linear) and feature learning (non-linear) regimes on subgroups of examples based on their difficulty. Specifically, we show that easier examples are given more weight in feature learning mode, resulting in faster training compared to more difficult ones. In other words, the non-linear dynamics tends to sequentialize the learning of examples of increasing difficulty. We illustrate this phenomenon across different ways to quantify example difficulty, including c-score, label noise, and in the presence of easy-to-learn spurious correlations. Our results reveal a new understanding of how deep networks prioritize resources across example difficulty.

papers.title: Higher Embedding Dimension Creates a Stronger World Model for a Simple Sorting Task
papers.research_question: How does embedding dimension affect the emergence of an internal world model in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps?
papers.core_contribution: Higher embedding dimensions lead to more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations (world models) in transformers trained on a sorting task, even after task accuracy saturates at lower dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build simple, structured internal world models even in constrained reinforcement learning settings, and increased model capacity (embedding dimension) improves the quality of these internal representations beyond what is reflected by task accuracy alone.
papers.key_findings:
The last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of input tokens.
The chosen adjacent swap corresponds to the largest difference between consecutive values in the encoded global ordering.
Task accuracy saturates at relatively low embedding dimensions (around 6 for length 6 sequences), but the fidelity and robustness of the internal ordering representation continue to improve up to around dimension 30.
Higher embedding dimensions make the learned internal mechanisms more consistent across different training runs and random seeds.
Low-dimension agents can fall into a 'local greedy trap', failing to form a coherent global ordering representation, a failure mode that decreases with higher embedding dimensions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited in scope and scale, focusing only on adjacent transposition sorting with 1-2 layer, single-head transformers, and does not explore more complex architectures or richer environments.
Computational budget restricted the ability to test broader ranges of sequence lengths or larger training runs.
future_direction: Relax the adjacency constraint to allow arbitrary in-place swaps to see if transformers discover known efficient algorithms or novel heuristics.
Introduce stochasticity into the environment (e.g., noisy token values or partial observability) to test if the ordering circuit emerges under uncertainty.
Explore hybrid training setups (e.g., supervised pre-training on optimal swaps followed by RL fine-tuning) to see if the ordering representation becomes more robust.
Introduce multi-head attention to examine if different heads specialize in complementary subproblems.
Test the robustness of the identified circuits under pruning or quantization, and apply similar analyses to structurally richer algorithmic tasks (e.g., graph algorithms).
papers.abstract: We investigate how embedding dimension affects the emergence of an internal "world model" in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps. Models achieve high accuracy even with very small embedding dimensions, but larger dimensions yield more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations. In particular, higher embedding dimensions strengthen the formation of structured internal representation and lead to better interpretability. After hundreds of experiments, we observe two consistent mechanisms: (1) the last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of tokens; and (2) the selected transposition aligns with the largest adjacent difference of these encoded values. Our results provide quantitative evidence that transformers build structured internal world models and that model size improves representation quality in addition to end performance. We release our metrics and analyses, which can be used to probe similar algorithmic tasks.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Anatomy of Catastrophic Forgetting: Hidden Representations and Task Semantics
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting affect the hidden representations of neural networks, and how is it influenced by task semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that catastrophic forgetting is primarily driven by changes in deeper layers, and that forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in higher layers, mitigation methods stabilize these layers, and forgetting is maximized for tasks of intermediate similarity, providing a foundation for understanding and mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper layers are the primary source of forgetting in neural networks.
Forgetting mitigation methods like elastic weight consolidation and replay buffers act by stabilizing deeper layer representations.
Forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
Representational similarity (measured by CKA) between tasks is key to understanding forgetting.
A novel CIFAR-100 distribution shift task approximates realistic input distribution shift for studying forgetting.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in developing versatile machine learning systems is catastrophic forgetting: a model trained on tasks in sequence will suffer significant performance drops on earlier tasks. Despite the ubiquity of catastrophic forgetting, there is limited understanding of the underlying process and its causes. In this paper, we address this important knowledge gap, investigating how forgetting affects representations in neural network models. Through representational analysis techniques, we find that deeper layers are disproportionately the source of forgetting. Supporting this, a study of methods to mitigate forgetting illustrates that they act to stabilize deeper layers. These insights enable the development of an analytic argument and empirical picture relating the degree of forgetting to representational similarity between tasks. Consistent with this picture, we observe maximal forgetting occurs for task sequences with intermediate similarity. We perform empirical studies on the standard split CIFAR-10 setup and also introduce a novel CIFAR-100 based task approximating realistic input distribution shift.

papers.title: Adding Interpretable Attention to Neural Translation Models Improves Word Alignment
papers.research_question: How can high-accuracy word alignments be extracted from the activations of a state-of-the-art neural machine translation model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a simple extension to the Transformer architecture (an alignment layer) and a novel inference procedure using stochastic gradient descent to optimize attention activations, enabling unsupervised extraction of word alignments comparable to statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method of extending the Transformer with an alignment layer and using SGD-based attention optimization can extract meaningful word alignments in an unsupervised manner, achieving quality comparable to IBM Model 4 (Giza++) on two out of three tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an alignment layer to the Transformer decoder, which lacks skip connections and is forced to rely on encoder information, significantly improves word alignment quality over naively averaging attention activations.
Optimizing the attention activations via stochastic gradient descent to maximize the likelihood of the target word further improves alignment quality.
The proposed method achieves alignment error rates comparable to Giza++ on German-English and Romanian-English datasets.
The neural alignment models benefit more from symmetrizing bidirectional alignments than statistical methods, possibly due to using full source context but not full target context.
Using a combination of word embeddings and encoder output as the key/value representation in the alignment layer yields the best results.
papers.limitation: The method does not outperform Giza++ on the English-French dataset, which the authors attribute to the large portion of 'probable' alignment links in the reference set, which favors Giza++'s tendency to predict fewer alignments.
papers.abstract: Multi-layer models with multiple attention heads per layer provide superior translation quality compared to simpler and shallower models, but determining what source context is most relevant to each target word is more challenging as a result. Therefore, deriving high-accuracy word alignments from the activations of a state-of-the-art neural machine translation model is an open challenge. We propose a simple model extension to the Transformer architecture that makes use of its hidden representations and is restricted to attend solely on encoder information to predict the next word. It can be trained on bilingual data without word-alignment information. We further introduce a novel alignment inference procedure which applies stochastic gradient descent to directly optimize the attention activations towards a given target word. The resulting alignments dramatically outperform the naive approach to interpreting Transformer attention activations, and are comparable to Giza++ on two publicly available data sets.

papers.title: Luck Matters: Understanding Training Dynamics of Deep ReLU Networks
papers.research_question: How does training dynamics of deep ReLU networks lead to generalization, and how can it explain phenomena like over-parameterization, implicit regularization, and lottery tickets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework for training dynamics of deep ReLU networks in a teacher-student setting, showing that lucky nodes close to teacher nodes converge faster and irrelevant nodes' fan-out weights vanish, explaining phenomena like over-parameterization and lottery tickets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a theoretical framework that explains training dynamics of deep ReLU networks and provides insight into several empirical phenomena, with future work to extend the analysis to more general settings.
papers.key_findings:
Student nodes whose weights are initialized close to teacher nodes converge to them at a faster rate.
In over-parameterized regimes, a small set of lucky nodes converge to teacher nodes while the fan-out weights of other nodes converge to zero.
The framework explains multiple puzzling phenomena: over-parameterization, implicit regularization, lottery tickets, flat minima, and fitting both structured and random data.
BatchNorm biases in pre-trained VGG models are mostly negative, supporting the assumption of small overlapping teacher node activations.
Experiments on Gaussian data and CIFAR-10 validate the theoretical predictions.
papers.limitation:
Theorem 5 is limited to 2-layer networks; extension to multi-layer is future work.
Assumption 3 (small overlap between teacher nodes) may not always hold.
Finite datasets cause convergence to stall, unlike infinite data.
future_direction: Extend Theorem 5 to general multi-layer setting
Relax Assumption 3
Study more BatchNorm effects
papers.abstract: We analyze the dynamics of training deep ReLU networks and their implications on generalization capability. Using a teacher-student setting, we discovered a novel relationship between the gradient received by hidden student nodes and the activations of teacher nodes for deep ReLU networks. With this relationship and the assumption of small overlapping teacher node activations, we prove that (1) student nodes whose weights are initialized to be close to teacher nodes converge to them at a faster rate, and (2) in over-parameterized regimes and 2-layer case, while a small set of lucky nodes do converge to the teacher nodes, the fan-out weights of other nodes converge to zero. This framework provides insight into multiple puzzling phenomena in deep learning like over-parameterization, implicit regularization, lottery tickets, etc. We verify our assumption by showing that the majority of BatchNorm biases of pre-trained VGG11/16 models are negative. Experiments on (1) random deep teacher networks with Gaussian inputs, (2) teacher network pre-trained on CIFAR-10 and (3) extensive ablation studies validate our multiple theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: Dynamic Position Encoding for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can Transformers be improved by dynamically encoding target position information to enhance translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Dynamic Position Encoding (DPE), a novel method that generates embeddings containing target word position information to improve neural machine translation in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: DPE consistently outperforms baselines by helping the source side learn target position information, demonstrating the usefulness of dynamic position encoding in Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
DPE improves BLEU scores over the baseline Transformer Base and other position encoding methods.
The improvement is due to the injection of position information, not just additional parameters, as shown by comparisons with increased encoder layers.
DPE is effective across different language pairs and dataset sizes, including IWSLT-14 and WMT-14.
Ablation studies show that the position loss weight λ=0.5 provides the best balance for translation accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The alignment tool FastAlign may not handle all cases like Many-to-Many alignments and multi-word expressions perfectly.
Limited investment in linguistic preprocessing due to resource constraints.
future_direction: Design additional rules for handling different word alignment cases.
Investigate more precise alignment tools beyond FastAlign.
Explore injecting order information into other language processing models like dependency parsing or sequence tagging.
papers.abstract: Recurrent models have been dominating the field of neural machine translation (NMT) for the past few years. Transformers \citep{vaswani2017attention}, have radically changed it by proposing a novel architecture that relies on a feed-forward backbone and self-attention mechanism. Although Transformers are powerful, they could fail to properly encode sequential/positional information due to their non-recurrent nature. To solve this problem, position embeddings are defined exclusively for each time step to enrich word information. However, such embeddings are fixed after training regardless of the task and the word ordering system of the source or target language. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture with new position embeddings depending on the input text to address this shortcoming by taking the order of target words into consideration. Instead of using predefined position embeddings, our solution generates new embeddings to refine each word's position information. Since we do not dictate the position of source tokens and learn them in an end-to-end fashion, we refer to our method as dynamic position encoding (DPE). We evaluated the impact of our model on multiple datasets to translate from English into German, French, and Italian and observed meaningful improvements in comparison to the original Transformer.

papers.title: Visualizing the PHATE of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the internal geometry and learning dynamics of neural networks to understand why certain networks outperform others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces M-PHATE, a visualization method that reveals the internal geometry and learning dynamics of neural networks by capturing the evolution of hidden unit activations over training, providing insights into phenomena like catastrophic forgetting and generalization without needing validation data.
papers.conclusion: M-PHATE provides an interpretable visualization of neural network learning dynamics, offering unique insights into network performance and behavior that are not apparent from classical metrics like validation loss and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, showing rapid structural changes and crossing of unit trajectories when tasks switch.
Increased heterogeneity among hidden units in M-PHATE visualizations correlates with improved generalization performance, while networks that memorize (e.g., with random labels) show low heterogeneity.
M-PHATE outperforms standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., t-SNE, Isomap) in capturing both the dynamics and community structure of hidden units during training.
The method allows meaningful comparison of hidden units across different layers, as neurons from different layers frequently co-localize in the visualization.
M-PHATE can be applied using only training data, providing a way to understand generalization performance without access to a validation set.
papers.abstract: Understanding why and how certain neural networks outperform others is key to guiding future development of network architectures and optimization methods. To this end, we introduce a novel visualization algorithm that reveals the internal geometry of such networks: Multislice PHATE (M-PHATE), the first method designed explicitly to visualize how a neural network's hidden representations of data evolve throughout the course of training. We demonstrate that our visualization provides intuitive, detailed summaries of the learning dynamics beyond simple global measures (i.e., validation loss and accuracy), without the need to access validation data. Furthermore, M-PHATE better captures both the dynamics and community structure of the hidden units as compared to visualization based on standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., ISOMAP, t-SNE). We demonstrate M-PHATE with two vignettes: continual learning and generalization. In the former, the M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of "catastrophic forgetting" which is a major challenge for learning in task-switching contexts. In the latter, our visualizations reveal how increased heterogeneity among hidden units correlates with improved generalization performance. An implementation of M-PHATE, along with scripts to reproduce the figures in this paper, is available at https://github.com/scottgigante/M-PHATE.

papers.title: Attention Guided CAM: Visual Explanations of Vision Transformer Guided by Self-Attention
papers.research_question: How to provide a high-level semantic explanation for Vision Transformer's decisions with great localization performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided gradient analysis method for Vision Transformer that provides high-level semantic explanations with great localization performance by combining gradients propagated from the classification output with self-attention scores normalized by sigmoid.
papers.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided gradient analysis method provides a reliable explanation of ViT and achieves state-of-the-art performance in weakly-supervised object localization, making ViT more adaptable to tasks involving object localization.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method outperforms previous leading explainability methods (Attention Rollout and LRP-based) for ViT in weakly-supervised localization tasks across multiple datasets.
The method reduces the peak intensity problem in visualization heatmaps by normalizing self-attention scores with sigmoid instead of softmax.
The method successfully captures the full area of target objects and multiple instances within an image, providing more precise and faithful explanations.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformer(ViT) is one of the most widely used models in the computer vision field with its great performance on various tasks. In order to fully utilize the ViT-based architecture in various applications, proper visualization methods with a decent localization performance are necessary, but these methods employed in CNN-based models are still not available in ViT due to its unique structure. In this work, we propose an attention-guided visualization method applied to ViT that provides a high-level semantic explanation for its decision. Our method selectively aggregates the gradients directly propagated from the classification output to each self-attention, collecting the contribution of image features extracted from each location of the input image. These gradients are additionally guided by the normalized self-attention scores, which are the pairwise patch correlation scores. They are used to supplement the gradients on the patch-level context information efficiently detected by the self-attention mechanism. This approach of our method provides elaborate high-level semantic explanations with great localization performance only with the class labels. As a result, our method outperforms the previous leading explainability methods of ViT in the weakly-supervised localization task and presents great capability in capturing the full instances of the target class object. Meanwhile, our method provides a visualization that faithfully explains the model, which is demonstrated in the perturbation comparison test.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: Deconstructing Positional Information: From Attention Logits to Training Biases
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding schemes (additive vs. multiplicative) mediate the interaction between token content and position, and what causes the performance paradox and single-head deposit pattern in RoPE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified Toeplitz-matrix framework to analyze positional encodings, discovers the single-head deposit pattern in RoPE, and provides a theoretical explanation showing this pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE's multiplicative structure.
papers.conclusion: The Toeplitz framework provides a powerful lens for understanding positional encodings, and the deposit pattern explains RoPE's performance paradox. Controlled mixing of positional signals is a promising strategy for achieving robust, distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's multiplicative structure enables superior performance on tasks requiring content-position coupling but leads to a single-head deposit pattern where positional information is concentrated in one early-layer head.
Additive positional encodings (Absolute, T5, ALiBi) do not exhibit the deposit pattern and show different learning dynamics.
The deposit pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE, caused by exponential amplification of gradient signals during training, leading to extreme specialization.
Hybrid architectures like Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) can mitigate the deposit pattern and improve robustness by mixing positional signals.
RoPE's strong inductive bias suppresses the formation of latent positional representations observed in models with additive or no PE.
papers.limitation:
The connection between the deposit pattern and RoPE's known struggles with length extrapolation requires direct empirical validation.
Future work should probe the limits of these positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks such as sequence reversal or Dyck language recognition.
future_direction: Direct empirical validation of the link between the deposit pattern and length extrapolation.
Testing positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks.
More complex controlled analysis of positional mechanisms in transformers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings enable Transformers to incorporate sequential information, yet their theoretical understanding remains limited to two properties: distance attenuation and translation invariance. Because natural language lacks purely positional data, the interplay between positional and semantic information is still underexplored. We address this gap by deconstructing the attention-logit computation and providing a structured analysis of positional encodings, categorizing them into additive and multiplicative forms. The differing properties of these forms lead to distinct mechanisms for capturing positional information. To probe this difference, we design a synthetic task that explicitly requires strong integration of positional and semantic cues. As predicted, multiplicative encodings achieve a clear performance advantage on this task. Moreover, our evaluation reveals a hidden training bias: an information aggregation effect in shallow layers that we term the single-head deposit pattern. Through ablation studies and theoretical analysis, we proved that this phenomenon is inherent in multiplicative encodings. These findings deepen the understanding of positional encodings and call for further study of their training dynamics.

papers.title: How Instruction and Reasoning Data shape Post-Training: Data Quality through the Lens of Layer-wise Gradients
papers.research_question: How do instruction and reasoning data of varying quality affect the layer-wise gradients during LLM post-training, and can existing data quality metrics be unified by spectral properties of these gradients?
papers.core_contribution: This work shows that various data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) can be unified by spectral properties of layer-wise gradients, specifically lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for higher-quality data, with effective rank being more robust. It also reveals that reasoning data induces higher effective ranks than instruction data.
papers.conclusion: Spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients provides a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, offering insights into training stability and data exploration strategies for post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Existing data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) are unified by consistent spectral properties of gradients: lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for high-quality data.
Effective rank outperforms nuclear norm in distinguishing low- vs. high-quality data and is more sensitive to subtle quality differences.
Reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, indicating richer gradient structures for complex tasks.
Within the same model family, layer-wise gradient spectral properties remain consistent across different model sizes, but diverge significantly across distinct model families.
Cosine similarities between gradients (same-layer and adjacent-layer) remain nearly zero and cannot reflect data quality.
papers.abstract: As the post-training of large language models (LLMs) advances from instruction-following to complex reasoning tasks, understanding how different data affect finetuning dynamics remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients induced by low/high-quality instruction and reasoning data for LLM post-training. Our analysis reveals that widely-studied metrics for data evaluation, e.g., IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, and Reward, can be explained and unified by spectral properties computed from gradients' singular value decomposition (SVD). Specifically, higher-quality data are usually associated with lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks. Notably, effective rank exhibits better robustness and resolution than nuclear norm in capturing subtle quality differences. For example, reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, implying richer gradient structures on more complex tasks. Our experiments also highlight that models within the same family share similar gradient patterns regardless of their sizes, whereas different model families diverge significantly. Providing a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, this work illuminates the interplay between data quality and training stability, shedding novel insights into developing better data exploration strategies for post-training.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: How connectivity structure shapes rich and lazy learning in neural circuits
papers.research_question: How does the structure of initial weights, particularly their effective rank, influence the network learning regime (rich vs lazy)?
papers.core_contribution: High-rank initializations typically yield lazier learning (smaller network changes), while low-rank initializations bias learning towards richer learning, except when the low-rank initialization aligns with task statistics, which can still lead to lazy learning.
papers.conclusion: Initial weight structure, particularly effective rank, plays a pivotal role in shaping learning regimes, with implications for metabolic costs of plasticity and risks of catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-rank random initialization leads to effectively lazier learning on average across tasks.
Low-rank initial weights (via SVD or biologically motivated structures) lead to effectively richer learning in RNNs.
Low-rank initialization aligned with task statistics (e.g., dominant features) can still achieve high kernel alignment and lazy learning.
Biologically motivated low-rank connectivity structures (e.g., Dale's law, chain motifs) exhibit lower effective rank and lead to richer learning compared to random Gaussian initialization.
Theoretical analysis in a two-layer linear network confirms that expected kernel alignment across tasks is maximized with high-rank initialization.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is conducted in simplified settings (linear feedforward networks) and may not fully capture the complexity of RNNs.
future_direction: Investigating the relationship between learning regimes and various concepts of dynamical regimes.
Exploring the impact of enforcing connectivity structures (e.g., Dale's law) throughout training.
Extending the analysis to a broader range of architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: In theoretical neuroscience, recent work leverages deep learning tools to explore how some network attributes critically influence its learning dynamics. Notably, initial weight distributions with small (resp. large) variance may yield a rich (resp. lazy) regime, where significant (resp. minor) changes to network states and representation are observed over the course of learning. However, in biology, neural circuit connectivity could exhibit a low-rank structure and therefore differs markedly from the random initializations generally used for these studies. As such, here we investigate how the structure of the initial weights -- in particular their effective rank -- influences the network learning regime. Through both empirical and theoretical analyses, we discover that high-rank initializations typically yield smaller network changes indicative of lazier learning, a finding we also confirm with experimentally-driven initial connectivity in recurrent neural networks. Conversely, low-rank initialization biases learning towards richer learning. Importantly, however, as an exception to this rule, we find lazier learning can still occur with a low-rank initialization that aligns with task and data statistics. Our research highlights the pivotal role of initial weight structures in shaping learning regimes, with implications for metabolic costs of plasticity and risks of catastrophic forgetting.

papers.title: A Memory-Augmented Neural Network Model of Abstract Rule Learning
papers.research_question: How can neural networks learn and apply abstract rules to novel contexts, specifically through arbitrary role-filler binding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Emergent Symbol Binding Network (ESBN), a memory-augmented neural network that learns to use an external memory as a binding mechanism, enabling symbol-like variable representations to emerge and allowing perfect generalization of abstract rules to novel fillers.
papers.conclusion: The ESBN demonstrates a capacity for arbitrary role-filler binding and abstract rule learning, and the factorization of memory into keys and values is an important inductive prior for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The ESBN achieves near-perfect generalization to novel fillers in both generative and multiple-choice modes, even when trained on only three fillers.
Standard LSTM and NTM models fail to generalize to novel fillers, especially as the number of withheld fillers increases.
The segregation of keys and values in the external memory is crucial for abstract rule learning and generalization.
The ESBN can learn abstract rules from limited experience, similar to humans.
papers.limitation:
There is a gray area in categorizing a filler as truly 'novel' since distinctness is often defined on a spectrum, especially in image space.
The model does not have a mechanism for dynamically unbinding, which may be inconsistent with some theories of working memory.
future_direction: Extend to other datasets like MNIST and ImageNet.
Extend to other RPM relations and existing RPM datasets.
Test other proposed models on our dataset.
papers.abstract: Human intelligence is characterized by a remarkable ability to infer abstract rules from experience and apply these rules to novel domains. As such, designing neural network algorithms with this capacity is an important step toward the development of deep learning systems with more human-like intelligence. However, doing so is a major outstanding challenge, one that some argue will require neural networks to use explicit symbol-processing mechanisms. In this work, we focus on neural networks' capacity for arbitrary role-filler binding, the ability to associate abstract "roles" to context-specific "fillers," which many have argued is an important mechanism underlying the ability to learn and apply rules abstractly. Using a simplified version of Raven's Progressive Matrices, a hallmark test of human intelligence, we introduce a sequential formulation of a visual problem-solving task that requires this form of binding. Further, we introduce the Emergent Symbol Binding Network (ESBN), a recurrent neural network model that learns to use an external memory as a binding mechanism. This mechanism enables symbol-like variable representations to emerge through the ESBN's training process without the need for explicit symbol-processing machinery. We empirically demonstrate that the ESBN successfully learns the underlying abstract rule structure of our task and perfectly generalizes this rule structure to novel fillers.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
papers.research_question: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theory and algorithms based on neuron activation subspace match to analyze representation similarity in neural networks, and finds that representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as expected.
papers.conclusion: Representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as prevalently expected, raising fundamental questions about learning representations and interpretability in deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum match similarity is low for most convolutional layers, indicating low overall similarity of representations.
Layers close to input and output show higher similarity due to alignment with input data and output targets, respectively.
Simple matches are rarely of small size, indicating that single neurons or small neuron clusters do not learn similar representations.
The structure of matches can be characterized by maximum matches and simple matches, which can be found efficiently with the proposed algorithms.
The findings raise questions about whether networks learn completely different representations or if subspace match is not the right metric for similarity.
papers.limitation: Subspace match may not be the right metric for measuring the similarity of representations.
papers.abstract: It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive, there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations. Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

papers.title: WeightScale: Interpreting Weight Change in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do different layers in neural networks converge to their learned features at different times during training? The paper investigates this using Relative Weight Change and clustering to analyze layer-wise learning dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an approach that combines Relative Weight Change with clustering and dimensionality reduction to interpret layer-wise learning dynamics in deep neural networks, scaling analysis to very deep architectures.
papers.conclusion: The paper enhances the RWC interpretability metric with clustering and dimensionality reduction, enabling analysis of layer-wise learning in deep networks and providing insights into learning dynamics across architectures and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Task complexity affects layer-wise learning: easier tasks like CIFAR-10 show decreased RWC in later layers, while harder tasks like CIFAR-100 show increased recruitment of later layers.
Clustering RWC trends allows identification of similar behaving layer groups and outliers in deep networks.
Different architectural primitives (e.g., depthwise vs. pointwise convolutions) exhibit distinct learning dynamics as measured by RWC.
The proposed method scales RWC analysis to very deep networks like EfficientNet-B4.
papers.limitation:
K-Means clustering struggles with noisy data and outliers, necessitating manual outlier removal.
The RWC metric has small differences between layers, limiting its ability to distinguish learning trends.
future_direction: Analyzing learning trends in ImageNet scale datasets
Extending to new modalities like NLP
Applying to a variety of architectures
papers.abstract: Interpreting the learning dynamics of neural networks can provide useful insights into how networks learn and the development of better training and design approaches. We present an approach to interpret learning in neural networks by measuring relative weight change on a per layer basis and dynamically aggregating emerging trends through combination of dimensionality reduction and clustering which allows us to scale to very deep networks. We use this approach to investigate learning in the context of vision tasks across a variety of state-of-the-art networks and provide insights into the learning behavior of these networks, including how task complexity affects layer-wise learning in deeper layers of networks.

papers.title: Diagnosing Catastrophe: Large parts of accuracy loss in continual learning can be accounted for by readout misalignment
papers.research_question: What representational changes underlie catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, and what processes account for the performance decrease?
papers.core_contribution: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is largely due to misalignment between hidden representations and readout layers, rather than loss of information in the representations.
papers.conclusion: Information in hidden layers is largely preserved during continual learning, and catastrophic forgetting may be efficiently addressed by solving readout misalignment without restricting learning of new tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Performance degradation in continual learning is primarily caused by readout misalignment, not by loss of task-relevant information in hidden representations.
Representational geometry is partially conserved under misalignment, with Procrustes alignment recovering about half of the performance drop.
Only a small fraction of information is irrecoverably lost (true forgetting).
Representational changes (misalignment, geometry change, forgetting) scale with the dimensionality of hidden representations.
Feature transfer from previous tasks contributes to performance on new tasks, but newly learned features provide additional, preserved information.
future_direction: Test the analysis framework for characterizing representational changes in continual learning on biological data.
papers.abstract: Unlike primates, training artificial neural networks on changing data distributions leads to a rapid decrease in performance on old tasks. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we investigate the representational changes that underlie this performance decrease and identify three distinct processes that together account for the phenomenon. The largest component is a misalignment between hidden representations and readout layers. Misalignment occurs due to learning on additional tasks and causes internal representations to shift. Representational geometry is partially conserved under this misalignment and only a small part of the information is irrecoverably lost. All types of representational changes scale with the dimensionality of hidden representations. These insights have implications for deep learning applications that need to be continuously updated, but may also aid aligning ANN models to the rather robust biological vision.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods for Multisensory Integration in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How do early training dynamics affect a neural network's ability to integrate information from multiple sources, and do deep networks exhibit critical learning periods for multisensory integration similar to biological systems?
papers.core_contribution: Deep networks exhibit critical learning periods for multisensory integration where early exposure to properly correlated signals is crucial, and cross-sensor reconstruction objectives can make learning more robust to such periods.
papers.conclusion: Critical learning periods for multi-source integration exist in deep networks across architectures and tasks, and training should be performed across modalities from the outset rather than pre-training separate backbones.
papers.key_findings:
Deep networks show critical learning periods for multisensory integration: temporary deficits early in training can permanently impair the ability to integrate sources.
Shallow networks do not exhibit such critical periods.
Even deep linear networks exhibit critical periods, indicating complex early dynamics contrary to wide-network linearization theories.
The introduced Relative Source Variance (RSV) measure reveals that deficits lead to polarized representations where units become selective to only one source.
Auxiliary cross-sensor reconstruction objectives stabilize learning dynamics and prevent critical periods, suggesting a reason for the success of self-supervised multi-modal training.
papers.limitation: The study focused on homogeneous sources (stereo, video) and did not investigate asymmetry between sources (e.g., different informativeness or ease).
future_direction: Study the role of asymmetry between sources (e.g., different informativeness or ease).
papers.abstract: We show that the ability of a neural network to integrate information from diverse sources hinges critically on being exposed to properly correlated signals during the early phases of training. Interfering with the learning process during this initial stage can permanently impair the development of a skill, both in artificial and biological systems where the phenomenon is known as a critical learning period. We show that critical periods arise from the complex and unstable early transient dynamics, which are decisive of final performance of the trained system and their learned representations. This evidence challenges the view, engendered by analysis of wide and shallow networks, that early learning dynamics of neural networks are simple, akin to those of a linear model. Indeed, we show that even deep linear networks exhibit critical learning periods for multi-source integration, while shallow networks do not. To better understand how the internal representations change according to disturbances or sensory deficits, we introduce a new measure of source sensitivity, which allows us to track the inhibition and integration of sources during training. Our analysis of inhibition suggests cross-source reconstruction as a natural auxiliary training objective, and indeed we show that architectures trained with cross-sensor reconstruction objectives are remarkably more resilient to critical periods. Our findings suggest that the recent success in self-supervised multi-modal training compared to previous supervised efforts may be in part due to more robust learning dynamics and not solely due to better architectures and/or more data.

papers.title: Understanding the Countably Infinite: Neural Network Models of the Successor Function and its Acquisition
papers.research_question: How do children learn the successor function, what latent number representations make this possible, and what does it mean to understand the countably infinite?
papers.core_contribution: The place-value model shows a drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries, revealing that counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, and curriculum learning shows sharpening of smaller number representations during development.
papers.conclusion: This study is a first step in using neural networks to understand the successor function, and future work should explore recurrent architectures for modeling the counting process more generally.
papers.key_findings:
The count list model achieved perfect training accuracy but 0% test accuracy, indicating no generalization.
The place-value model showed 24% test accuracy and sensitivity to tens boundaries in representational similarity.
MDS analysis revealed systematic mapping of numbers to successors across tens boundaries in the place-value model.
Curriculum learning simulations showed incremental learning and sharpening of representations for smaller numbers.
The models did not learn the successor function well for the highest test range (81-99) in curriculum learning.
papers.limitation:
The count list model lacks sensitivity to tens boundaries, which is critical for place-value structure.
The place-value model has low test accuracy (24%) and does not generalize perfectly.
The models learn formally different ML tasks, making direct comparison difficult.
In curriculum learning, the highest test range (81-99) was not learned well even with additional training.
future_direction: Move beyond generating the successor of a number to modeling the counting process more generally.
Explore training recurrent neural network models to sequentially count, first to 100 and then arbitrarily high.
Use richer recurrent architectures to learn the recursive structure of natural numbers.
papers.abstract: As children enter elementary school, their understanding of the ordinal structure of numbers transitions from a memorized count list of the first 50-100 numbers to knowing the successor function and understanding the countably infinite. We investigate this developmental change in two neural network models that learn the successor function on the pairs (N, N+1) for N in (0, 98). The first uses a one-hot encoding of the input and output values and corresponds to children memorizing a count list, while the second model uses a place-value encoding and corresponds to children learning the language rules for naming numbers. The place-value model showed a predicted drop in representational similarity across tens boundaries. Counting across a tens boundary can be understood as a vector operation in 2D space, where the numbers with the same tens place are organized in a linearly separable manner, whereas those with the same ones place are grouped together. A curriculum learning simulation shows that, in the expanding numerical environment of the developing child, representations of smaller numbers continue to be sharpened even as larger numbers begin to be learned. These models set the stage for future work using recurrent architectures to move beyond learning the successor function to simulating the counting process more generally, and point towards a deeper understanding of what it means to understand the countably infinite.

papers.title: Fast weight programming and linear transformers: from machine learning to neurobiology
papers.core_contribution: This primer reviews Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), a family of recurrent neural networks with matrix-form hidden states, and discusses their computational characteristics, connections to transformers and state space models, and potential relevance to models of synaptic plasticity in the brain.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that FWPs offer a powerful framework for sequence modeling with connections to transformers and state space models, and may provide insights into neural computation and synaptic plasticity in the brain.
papers.key_findings:
FWPs are recurrent neural networks with two-dimensional matrix-form hidden states that can be interpreted as fast, dynamically changing synaptic weights, serving as short-term memory storage.
FWPs are mathematically equivalent to linear transformers and can be seen as a form of fast weight programming, where a slow network programs the fast weights of another network.
Different update rules for FWPs, such as the delta rule, lead to different expressivity properties, with some variants capable of handling state-tracking tasks like parity and modular arithmetic.
FWPs provide a framework for understanding in-context learning as a form of fast weight programming, where the model adapts its fast weights based on input demonstrations.
FWPs may offer a biologically plausible model of synaptic plasticity and rapid synaptic modulation in the brain, bridging artificial neural networks and neurobiology.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in artificial neural networks for machine learning, and language modeling in particular, have established a family of recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures that, unlike conventional RNNs with vector-form hidden states, use two-dimensional (2D) matrix-form hidden states. Such 2D-state RNNs, known as Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), can be interpreted as a neural network whose synaptic weights (called fast weights) dynamically change over time as a function of input observations, and serve as short-term memory storage; corresponding synaptic weight modifications are controlled or programmed by another network (the programmer) whose parameters are trained (e.g., by gradient descent). In this Primer, we review the technical foundations of FWPs, their computational characteristics, and their connections to transformers and state space models. We also discuss connections between FWPs and models of synaptic plasticity in the brain, suggesting a convergence of natural and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state.
